As there is a very great shortage of potatoes at the present time in different parts of Ontario, both for food and seed purposes, 1 should be glad if one of the ministers, possibly the Minister of Agriculture, who stated some time ago that there was a large surplus of potatoes in different parts of Canada, would tell us where these surplus potatoes can be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The condition of the potato industry, very briefly, is this: When we heard of reported shortages and a scarcity in some parts of the country, I communi-oalted wlith every provincial Minister of Agriculture in Canada to ascertain as closely as he could the conditions in his own province; this was at the end of February. As nearly as we could ascertain, a conservative estimate put it at about one and a half million bushels surplus over and above the food and seed requirements of the whole country. The surpluses were chiefly in the provinces of Alberta, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. In some other provinces shortages were reported, and other provinces were not quite sure. We checked up the figures at the end of March by .following all the exports from the country, and again up to the 15th of April, and from the time we estimated the amount of potatoes in the country up to the 15th April about half a million bushels were exported, leaving-if our estimate was at all correct, and it was based on the information I have indicated-about one million bushels surplus still in this country. Of course that may be only approximate. I might also say to my hon. friend that a summary of all the replies I received was sent to each Minister of Agriculture in the different provinces, in order that he might know the exact condition throughout the country, together with ithe suggestion that it might be advisable for those ministers whose provinces were likely to be short, to watch the situation as closely as possible with the idea of doing what they could to supply the needs of their own province.

The consideration of the proposed motion of Hon. Sir Thomas White (Minister of

Finance) for the Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment of Mr. Turriff thereto, was resumed from Friday, April 27.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
By Order in Council, under authority of the War Measures Act, the Government, on 16th April, placed upon the free list three commodities, wheat, wheat flour and semolina, and by that action brought into operation the provision of the Underwood Tariff under which wheat and wheat products from the coun-' try taking such action become entitled to free entry to the markets of the United States. The matter was not referred to in the Budget but my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has moved an amendment, and it is to that amendment and to the subject of free wheat that I purpose for a short time to give consideration. It seems to me that the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite with reference to this action of the Government in placing wheat, wheat flour and semolina on the free list is a most extraordinary one. These hon. gentlemen have asserted for the last three years-the Underwood Tariff having come into effect in October, 1913-that they were in favour of free wheat. One would have thought that when the Government took the action which has been taken these hon. gentlemen would rejoice. One would have thought that the hon. member for Assiniboia, and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) when speaking on the question, would at least have looked pleased. The impression goes out from the House that hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken on this question are glad that the Government has taken this action, but to us in the House they do not look glad, they appear to be sorry. I wonder if the real explanation is not that these hon. gentlemen prefer to have the cry rather than the wool, that they would rather have free wheat ,as a political issue rather than free wheat as an actuality. At all events, that seems like a reasonable explanation of their attitude on the action of the Government in placing these three commodities on the free list and calling into operation the provision in the Underwood Tariff that I have mentioned.
The criticism of the Opposition upon the action of the Government in this regard proceeds upon several grounds. First, they say it was a departure from the fiscal policy of the Government and of the Conservative
party. Second, they say: You have granted it now; why did you not grant it before the war? Third, they say: You grant it now during the war, why did you not grant it earlier in the war? Fourth, they say: The measure is temporary, and with the end of the war the duties are automatically restored. And fifth, they have the temerity to say that the Government was actuated by political consideration in view of an approaching election. I am sure my ears did not fail me and that I distinctly heard my hon. friend from Assiniboia make that last statement.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You are quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
admits it. Now let me say-because I desire to discuss this matter seriously and earnestly-that we on this side, ever since the Underwood Tariff came into effect in 1913, have viewed this matter of free wheat upon what we regarded as its merits; we have never declined to grant free wheat on the ground that it involved a departure from the traditional fiscal policy of the Conservative party. I proceed now to prove that what I state is correct. In the Budget speech of 1914, which was the first occasion upon which I discussed the Underwood Tariff in the House of Commons, I set forth the arguments pro and con on the subject of free wheat; I set them out fully, I set them out, I submit, judicially; I did not take the ground that the Government would have nothing to do with this because it was a violation of the fiscal policy of the Conservative party. I examined the whole question from a business, economic, and public standpoint. I said:
So much for these opposing arguments and contentions. Speaking generally, it is not advisable that a nation's tariff should be so arranged as to fit into the particular features of that of another nation. This, however, would not be a conclusive reason for not making a change clearly in the national interest.
At that time we came to the conclusion, having regard to the fluctuations of price between Winnipeg, Minneapolis and Chicago, that there was not the advantage to the farmer that was claimed in this matter of free wheat* and, having regard to other considerations-industries in Canada of an important character and the condition of our railways-we thought it was not advisable at that time to grant free wheat. But we did not argue it upon the ground that it would be a departure from the fiscal policy of the Conservative party. On tlie contrary, we said by implication that if it

were in the national interest we were prepared to consider it. I desire to make that perfectly clear. Let us see what I said when this matter was before the House in February, 1916. I spoke on a resolution moved by the hon. member (Mr. Turriff), who now brings forward this amendment. 1 had been giving the matter my most painstaking attention during the whole of the year. If the Government held the view at that time that it was a departure from the fiscal policy to consider this question, what would be the reason for my giving consideration to the matter in my office continuously as I did? This is what I said, as reported in Hansard on page 861, February 16, 1916:-
I have caused a record to he kept of prices of grain both in Canada and in the United States, with a view to thoroughly familiarizing myself with the merits of the question in order to reach a sound and just conclusion in the national interest. When I say in the national interest, I need not say how important a factor in the national interest I consider the interest and material well-being of the three great grain-growing provinces of the West. It is in that spirit that I have approached, from time to time, the consideration of this question.
And I expressed the opinion on that occasion, in February, 1916. that it was unwise in the national interest that free wheat should be granted. It was not clear to me that the advantages that would be gained would outweigh the disadvantages, but I repeat, and the point I am making is that we always considered the question upon its merits and had regard, in dealing with it, only to what we regarded as the national interest. The position of the Government, in its view upon the question of free wheat in 1914, in 1916, and in April of this year, when we took action, has been absolutely sound and consistent throughout. I make that statement without the slightest hesitation ; I say our action has been sound and consistent throughout. How can it be urged that it was a violation of Conservative fiscal policy? Sir John A. Macdonald was a fairly good Conservative; so I have heard. Sir Leonard Tilley was the finance minister of Sir John A. Macdonald. Sir Leonard Tilley introduced the National Policy budget about 1879. The National Policy budget of 1879 has 'been the charter of the fiscal policy of the Conservative party from that day to this. Let us see what Sir Leonard Tilley said in regard to reciprocal provisions in the tariff. Sir Leonard Tilley, in 1879, in introducing the National Policy budget, said:-
The Government, requiring more revenue, have determined to ask this House to impose
[Sir Thomas White.!
upon the products of the United States that have been free, such a duty as may seem consistent with our position. But the Government couple with the proposal, in order to show that we approach this question with no unfriendly spirit, a resolution that will be laid on the table containing a proposition to this effect: That, as to articles named, which are the natural products of the country, including lumber, if the United States take off the duties in part or in whole, we are prepared to meet them with equal concessions. The Government believe in a reciprocity tariff, yet may discuss Free Trade or Protection, but the question of to-day is-Shall we have a reciprocity tariff, or a one-sided tariff?	[DOT]
That was the National Policy budget of Sir Leonard Tilley in 1879. Is it contrary to the fiscal policy of the Conservative party either to have a reciprocity provision in the tariff which remains under you control absolutely or to take advantage of a reciprocal provision in the tariff of another country? I submit that the action of Sir Leonard Tilley in 1879 is absolutely conclusive evidence that the attitude we have taken is in no way inconsistent with the fiscal policy of the Conservative party.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No; it was the election that you were thinking of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have a great
personal regard for my right hon. friend. He weathered the storm for many years and he was always on firm ground when he followed the policy of Sir Leonard Tilley. My right hon. friend notwithstanding his free trade professions in 1893, when he got into office followed in the footsteps of Sir John Macdonald and Sir Leonard Tilley and while he continued in that path he got on well in regard to his fiscal policy. But, my right hon. friend instead of continuing to follow the true lights was allured by a will-of-the-wisp and that brings me to the reciprocity agreement of 1911. My right hon. friend I think, would admit, if he would tell us his opinion candidly, that he then made a political mistake of the first magnitude

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: He did nothing of the kind. The policy of Sir Leonard Tilley in 1879 was that reciprocity of tariff would conduce to reciprocity of trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am sorry that my right hon. friend has not got over 1911. He tried upon that occasion to prove the impossible. He tried to prove that under reciprocity the farmer would get more for his product but that the consumer would pay less. We all kn.ow that when my right hon friend attempted to prove that to the people of Canada he was fore-doomed to

failure. Not even my right hon. friend could do that. He could not pr.ove the impossible. My right hon. friend in connection with the reciprocity agreement, was like a mariner who disregarded the beacon lights. He disregarded the beacon light that was hung up by one of the greatest Liberals of the day, Hon. George Brown. When the Hon. George Brown was a member of the coalition government formed to bring about Confederation, he went to Washington in connection with the matter of reciprocity and he absolutely declined to become a party to an agreement such as was entered into by my right hon. friend's Government with the Government at Washington. Hon. George Brown stated that every tariff agitation over there would find its echo at Ottawa and 'he actually resigned from the coalition Government upon that ground. You will find authority for that in the letters and memoirs of the Hon. George Brown.
There were many objections to the reciprocity agreement as has been shown by our experience in 1911. Quite a number of articles, which, under the agreement would nave entered the United States, subject to duty, enter the United States to-day free. I repeat there were many objections to the reciprocity agreement. The chief objection was the fact of the agreement. It is true that on its face it was stated that it was not a treaty, but in substance and in fact it was a treaty and when it was entered into the late Government lost to a considerable degree the control of its own tariff. That was the feature of the reciprocity agreement, to which chief objection was taken. There were many other objections but that was one of the chief ones, and it was, that when that agreement was entered into the Government of Canada lost in a measure the control .of its own tariff. Under the National Policy Budget of 1879, Sir Leonard Tilley did not lose control of his tariff for a moment, and in the action which we have taken under the authority of the War Measures Act, we have not for one moment lost control of our tariff.
Our action was not preceded by any negotiations There was no agreement with the United States. We took action under the War Measures Act, and we placed wheat and wheat flour and semolina on the free list. The tariff is just as much under the control of this Parliament as it was on April fifteenth. There is a clear distinction between taking advantage of reciprocal provisions in the tariff of another country or
offering advantages by reciprocal provision in your own tariff, control of which you do not lose for a moment, and negotiating an agreement under which you lose such control. That is a clear distinction that any one can make.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If, under the agreement of 1911, Canada would have lost control of her tariff, would the United States have lost control of its tariff under that agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It would to a certain extent, but not to the extent that Canada would. The United States was a very much larger country than Canada and there would not be the same considerations weighing with the Government of the United States contemplating the recision of agreement that there would have been upon the Government of Canada considering recision.
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) should have made a fresh start after 1911; he should have Said: I have made a mistake with regard to reciprocity, and I am going to make a new start. I often think that my right hon. friend was more partial to the reciprocity agreement than to any other child of his political brain. One reason was that it was the youngest. Reciprocity was my right hon. friend's youngest political child, and we must not blame him from being partial to it, because it was his Benjamin. I mention that because, like parents whose children who have been lost, my right hon. friend sees resemblances to reciprocity in many measures brought forward in this House. For example, if I borrow in New York my right hon. friend says: Oh, that is reciprocity.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No, that is truck and trade with the Yankees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says that is truck and trade with the Yankees and he has said in this House that it was. But it is not his long lost child, reciprocity; it is a very much more healthy and robust infant; it is legitimate business, borrowing in the United States, just as I might borrow in Great Britain. We sell our securities to the United States just as for generations past we have sold goods to the United States. But my right hon. friend sees in it a far away resemblance to reciprocity.
Then when we, under the War Measures Act, take the action which we have taken and bring into operation the reciprocal provision in the Underwood Tariff of 1913, my

right hon. friend again says: Reciprocity! But it is still a case of mistaken identity. This is a very much more self-respecting child than reciprocity or the reciprocity agreement of 1911 because, as I have pointed out, in this action that we have taken we have not lost for one moment control of our tariff. The fundamental and essential difference between our action respecting free wheat and the reciprocity agreement is that we retain in its fulness and entirety our control over our own tariff. We have not in the slightest degree abridged our freedom of fiscal action or surrendered one jot or tittle of our fiscal independence.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean by that that the Government can at any moment repeal this provision in regard to free wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I shall later on deal very fully with that criticism, which was made by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley).
The second criticism that is offered is this: Why do you do this now and not be-before the war? I answer: because conditions have been profoundly changed by the war. Conditions affecting trade, international conditions affecting ocean transport have been radically and profoundly changed. There has been a revolution in trade and in transportation methods and conditions since the outbreak of this-war. Let us take our condition three years ago, before war broke out. We exported largely to Great Britain. We borrowed largely in Great Britain, that is to say, we exported our securities and sold them there. We were obligated to pay in Great Britain interest upon huge sums which we had borrowed for the development of this country. We imported to a considerable extent from Great Britain. WTe imported to a large extent from the United States. Our imports from the United States greatly exceeded our exports to the United States. We were, I think, the second best customer of the United States. How did we pay the United States for the balance of trade? We paid the United States for the balance of trade through Great Britain. Great Britain exported to the LTnited States, and those exports would be a set off to her imports from the United States. But in addition to that the United States owed Great Britain vast sums for interest upon securities. In addition to that Great Britain, by the services of her carrying fleet, established a large indebted-
ness on the part of the United States. The result was, as I have stated, that it was England that paid the United States the balance that we owed the United States upon international trading. Now let us see what has happened since the war has broken out. Our imports from the United States have immensely increased.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My right hon. friend says "hear, hear."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes, our imports from the United States have immensely increased. How can we liquidate that^ adverse balance to-day with existing conditions of transportation and exchange between England and the United States unless we increase the sale of our products to the United States?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear, by all means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: At last my right hon. friend and I are together in agreement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is what reciprocity would have done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: But reciprocity was a peace time measure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am speaking about war conditions, and they have brought this about.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You seem very much involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Let us see what the conditions were in 1911, or even in 1914. My right hon. friend need not take my opinion or my statements; I shall cite to him one whose authority not even my right hon. friend will question. But let us see, just for a moment, the change that has taken place in the exchange of commodities between Gfeat Britain and the United States since the outbreak of this war. In 1914 the exports from the United States to Great Britain were $594,000,000, let us say $600,000,000, merchandise only, and in 1916, last year, those exports had risen to $1,500,000,000 from the United States to the United Kingdom, or an increase of $900,000,000 in favour of the United States as compared with pre-war exports.
At the same time, the exports of Great Britain to the United States had increased only from $293,000,000 to $308,000,000. This means that exchange has

completely broken down between the United Kingdom and the United States; that the conditions which prevailed before the war do not prevail to-day; that an entire change has taken place both as to the channels of trade and the conditions under which trade is carried on.
I told my bon. friend that I would quote an authority to which he would defer. At the Guildhall a few days ago, Mr. Lloyd George, Prime Minister of Great Britain, referring to the transportation situation and the food conditions in Great Britain, made a most important statement Speaking about the shortage of ocean transport and its effect in Great Britain, he said that arrangements were being made whereby imports would be cut down by over 10.000,000 tons yearly without interfering with any essential industry in Great Britain. Why is the Government of the United Kingdom devoting its energies to cutting down imports? Because of the shortage in tonnage brought about by submarine warfare. Sir Edward Carson said yesterday that the losses from submarines were growing. There is no use minimizing or blinking matters; the submarine menace is a terrible one. During the week before last 40 large British and a'jlied vessels and 15 smaller ones were sunk, to say nothing of neutral shipping. That is the condition with which we are confronted to-day: the submarine menace to British and neutral shipping; regulations as to food enforced in the United Kingdom. Mr. Lloyd George further said: " We are placing under Cultivation 3,000,000 fresh acres of land so that in 1918 we shall be able to support ourselves within the confines of the United Kingdom." Will that have any effect upon trade or upon imports of foodstuffs? This war has brought about a limitation of ordinary imports into Great Britain, and of exports from Great Britain. Every day of my life I am asked by some interest in Canada to see if I can get the embargo lifted whereby exports from Great Britain of commodities in which they are interested are prohibited from leaving the ports of the United Kingdom-the reason being, of course, the shortage of shipping.
Coming to the wheat question, wlhat does Lloyd George say? I direct the attention of my right hon. friend and of the member for Assiniboia to the following words:
There are 85,000,000 bushels of wheat in Canada-
That is an under-statement.
-I would not say for the asking, but for the fetching;. It ought to have been here. I believe that about twenty or thirty million bushels
of this wheat had to go to the United States for lack of another market. We must cut down our food until we discover a method of destroying this ocean bacillus. That is one thing that has got to be done.
The British Prime Minister then says that there is plenty of wheat in Canada, not for the asking, but for the fetching. He says:	It is impossible to fetch it on
account of the submarine mepace and of the shortage of shipping; consequently it has to find <a market in the United States. This indicates that formerly the wheat had
found a market in the United Kingdom,	
and that normally it would find its market there to-day if the British authorities had the shipping to fetch - it.
So far as conditions affecting the sale of Canadian wheat were formerly concerned, there was a good export demand from millers and others in the United Kingdom for all grades of our wheat. There was a better demand for the high grades, but there was, nevertheless, a demand for the lower grades. While there is still a certain demand locally and by millers for the low grades of Canadian wheat in our West, it is a fact that the export demand for low grade wheat has diminished-this is precisely what you would expect-because of the food regulations in the United Kingdom and the shortage of cargo space. They adopted regulations in the United Kingdom with a view to gerting the greatest amount of food product out of a given amount of grain. For a considerable part of the last few months Stoddart & Company, who have been purchasers for Great Britain of wheat in Canada, have been purchasing the higher grades of wheat-only recently have they been purchasing any of the lower grades-and the result was that while there was a good market for the higher grades of wheat, there was not as good a market for the lower grades. The hon. member for Assiniboia knows that.
In addition, it is perfectly clear to me that advantage was being taken of the situation with regard to the lower grades of wheat and that the farmer was not receiving for the lower grades of wheat the money that he should have received. That was the position with which the Government was confronted. If anybody is disposed to challenge that, let him examine the figures for March, which show in most illuminating fashion what has happened with regard to the channels of trade. In the month of March, 1916, 400,000 bushels of wheat only went from Canada to the United States, and in the same month of this year 2,400,000

bushels of wheat went into the United States-six times as much, an excess of 2,000,000 bushels. This occurred, as I have stated, because the exchange situation and the shortage of ocean transportation has given Canadian wheat and other products a tendency to move towards the United States.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Who paid the duty on that wheat going into the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It would have to be paid in every case, but there might be a drawback with respect to a good deal of it. I am unable to say how much, and 1 am sure that my hon. friend is unable to say how much. The fact remains, how ever-and it is a most illuminating fact- tint the increased amount of wheat going into the United States in the month of March of this year was as I have stated.
The hon. member for Assiniboia then makes his third criticism of the action of the Government. He says: "Why was not free wheat granted early in the war? If you did this owing to war conditions, why did you not do it in 1914?" But even the hon. member for Assiniboia would not have had the temerity to ask the Government in 1914-15 to grant free wheat, because the market at Winnipeg was so very much higher than the market at Minneapolis or Chicago. There was no resolution with regard to free wheat in 1914-15, immediately after the outbreak of war.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: We advocated it every year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend could not have advocated it in 1915, because, as a matter of fact, for many months in the fall of 1914 the market at Winnipeg was much higher than the market at Minneapolis or Chicago.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend shakes his head-but there is no doubt about it-that the market at Winnipeg was better, and there are reasons for that.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend not contrasting, say, No. 2 Northern Manitoba grade with No. 2 Northern Minneapolis grade?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No, I am familiar with all those distinctions..

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is what my hon. friend has done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I make the statement that after the outbreak of the war the Winnipeg market was better than either the Minneapolis market or the Chicago market.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
There were reasons for that. The exchange, instead of being favourable to the United States, as it is to-day, was unfavourable to the United States. That is sufficient answer to my hon. friend, who says: Well, if it is proper to do it in war time, why did you not do it earlier in the war? The reason was that conditions earlier in the war were such that the exchange was unfavourable to the United States.
We come down now to last year. It was uncertain, during last year, as to what the position was. Sometimes the price at Winnipeg would be a little higher than the price at Minneapolis; sometimes the price would be a little higher at Minneapolis than at Winnipeg. The statement was made here that on the lower grades of wheat there was a considerable spread. There was likely to be a greater spread on the lower grades at that time than on the higher grades, but that argument was put forward last year. There are, however, two considerations to be borne in mind. In the first place, the submarine menace had not yet developed on the scale that it is at the present time. It is a well known iact that during the early part of 1916 it was believed that the submarine menace had been mastered. I am speaking now of the small submarine. What has transpired since that is this: There has appeared upon the scene for many months the super-submarine with an enlarged area of operation, and it i3 the super-submarine and the multiplication of submarines toy Germany devoting the energies of her shipbuilding plants to the building of submarines that has brought about this acute situation. But it took a long time to develop; it was only on February 1 of this year that Germany declared a blockade of the British Isles and announced to the entire world that she would sink the shipping, not only of Great Britain but of neutrals. Up to that point she was sinking the shipping of Great Britain; she had not dared to sink the shipping, at all events, of that great neutral, the United States; but since February 1, she has been sinking, not only British shipping, but neutral shipping, and she has in that way profoundly affected the carrying capacity of the Atlantic fleets, although last year it was not apparent that the situation, which has since developed,

would develop. But there is another very important situation. The United States at that time was not an ally. It 4 p.m. might have been possible that Great Britain would require the entire wheat crop of Canada. What is the position to-day? The United States has taken her place with the Allies in this great war. The wheat and other food products of the United States and of Canada are practically pooled to-day for the use of the Allies. The British buyers, buying for Great Britain and for her Allies, are purchasing the exportable wheat crop of the United States and of Canada.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is that the reason why my hon. friend has put wheat on the free list?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I am developing this argument beautifully.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend cannot fail to understand. He who runs may read. I am giving my reasons why we did not do last year what we did in April this year.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: There is one you have not yet given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: And if my hon. friend's mind were open for a moment, he would understand and agree that the course which we have pursued has been, not only consistent, but beneficial.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Giving many reasons and fishing for a good one.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Those reasons do not tally with those given by the Solicitor General.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Our reasons
usually tally. The Solicitor General is usually correct in the facts, and I try also to be correct. I was amazed the other night to hear my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) actually jeer-not so much in express words, but by his manner-at the high prices which the farmers of the West are receiving for wheat. I would have thought, if my hon. friend rejoiced, as he stated that he rejoiced, at the placing of wheat, wheat flour and semolina upon the free list, thus giving access to the United States for our wheat and wheat products, he would at least look pleasant; but he did not; he was rather annoyed.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
He always looks
pleasant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: He is pretty good looking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: then all I have to say is that I should not like to see him when he is looking unpleasant.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The sadness of the Government's supporters would make anybody feel sad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend looked pleasant in just the same sense that a man having his photograph taken looks pleasant-my hon. friend knows what I mean by that. He had very little sympathy for the high prices the farmers in the West were getting for their wheat. We often hear statements made as to the energy which Governments should devote in order to bring immigrants into this country, and I agree with all that has been said as to the desirability of the greatest possible activity being shown in bringing immigrants into this country; but the best immigration agent for Canada is a good price for wheat.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The situation was the same last year as it is this year. Is that a new idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend the other night from his seat in the House rather jeered at the high prices which the farmers of the West were receiving for their wheat-

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Mr. Deputy Speaker, I leave it to you, Sir; you were in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better put it this way: I will not say that my hon. friend jeered at the high price of wheat; I will say that my hon. friend apparently had no sympathy with the high price which the farmer was obtaining for his wheat. The agricultural community is entitled to every possible consideration. Agriculture is the very base of our industrial fabric; the farmers are the real pro-

ducers; the pyramid rests squarely upon the base of agricultural production.' There is nothing too good for the farmers because they earn all they get ; they are not in any combines. I was raised on a farm; I know what it is to get up at five o'clock in the morning, and I know how the farmer earns his money. I know what he gets, he earns by hard work.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Some times he earns
what he does not get.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It is a good thing then that the farmer is getting a good price for his product. I do not know of anything that will relieve the high cost of living later more than the fact that there is a good price for agricultural products. What stimulates production is a good return for the effort expended and the capital invested; and that principle applies to agriculture as it does to any other business. I have no sympathy with stock exploitation, with stock gamblers or wheat gamblers, but I have great sympathy .with the farmer getting a proper price for his product.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Would my ton. friend be good enough to elaborate that idea and show how high prices for agricultural products will reduce the cost of living.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend tried and failed in 1911 to establish that very thesis.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: And the Minister of Finance argued the other way then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend was out ot the House when I pointed out that among other reasons why my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) signally failed in 1911, was that he attempted to prove to the intelligent people of this country that the farmer would get more for his product and the consumer would pay less. My hon. friend would hardly expect me to embark upon that undertaking after the example of 1911.
Another argument of my hon. friend was: Why should we do this at this time with the price of low grade wheat at a dollar or $1.30, as the case may be, as it only means ten cents a bushel to the farmer? Well, ten cents on fifty million bushels means $5,000,000, and on twenty-five million bushe'ls, $2,500,000. Does my hon. friend mean to say that if this is a proper course for us to take in the national interest at this time of war conditions, the farmer in the West is not entitled to that ten cents? That was practically the argument of my

hon. friend the other night, and I was surprised at him making it.
To come to another matter. It was argued in 1914 and in 1916 that the milling industry might be injuriously affected by such a measure as this. Now, there are few industries in Canada that have had greater profits since the outbreak of the war than the milling industry; enormous profits have been made by the large milling companies. It has been suggested on the other side of the House, what about railways, what about the transportation situation? . Well, the war has materially changed that also. The war has changed the entire situation in Canada. What is the situation so far as the railways are concerned? My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) knows that wheat is not being taken out of the West to-day as it should be.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Because of the
shortage of rolling stock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Because of the shortage of rolling stock and motive power.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: A farmer in the West told me within the last six weeks that he sold 50,000 bushels of wheat. He went down to New York and made arrangements for shipping it across the ocean, and he said that there were hundreds and hundreds of cars standing on every siding in his part of the country, and the railroads would not take them away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Because of the shortage of motive power and the blocking of the eastern lines and terminals. If my hon. friend desires information on that point, let him do what I did. I am not talking at random; I consulted the Chairman of the Railway Commission, and I know what the railway situation is in this country. Does my hon. friend mean to say that wheat is coming out of the Goose I.ake District to-day, and that there are not millions of bushels in the hands of the farmer that cannot be moved by reason of the blockade on our railways and the shortage of rolling stock? Let my hon. friend ask the Chairman of the Railway Commission what is the greatest need of railways to-day, and he will be told rolling stock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I ask my hon.
friend to go and see him.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I can only tell my hon. friend that if he travels along the roads in the west he will find hundreds and thousands of cars standing idle on the tracks. It is not a shortage of rolling stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
What is my
argument? I am showing that the railway situation has materially changed since the *war.	.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The trouble is the want of elevators at the Atlantic terminals. The St. John elevators were burnt three years ago, and have not been rebuilt yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: So on all grounds the action of the Government was the right and proper course to take, having regard to the conditions which existed at that time. My hon. friend has a further, criticism. He says: Why did you act under the War Measures Act? Why didn't you come down to Parliament and make these changes in your Budget? I think this Budget debate itself is a sufficient answer to that. How long will it be before this debate will close and before the measures which are now before the House will be enacted into law by this House and by the Senate? How long does it take to have Budiget proposals translated into legislation? They go into effect immediately, so far as the Customs Department is concerned, but as a matter of fact they do not become law until the legislation is passed by this House and by the Senate and the Governor General has given his consent.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
They go into practical
effect when the Budget speech is made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
They go into
practical effect, but they would not meet the conditions of the tariff of another country. Hon. gentlemen say that we should not have taken this step under the War Measures Act. They say we should have included this free wheat measure in the Budget, and debated it for a month or six weeks, and two months from now the proposals would be enacted into law. Supposing we had done that? It would mean that the farmer of the West would have been deprived all that time of ten cents a bushel in respect of the low grade wheat he exported to the United States. I believe myself that in a clear ease, where you are certain as to the propriety of what you are doing, what is called fer is action, if you have the power to take that action. My hon. friend's criticism that this action should lhave not have been taken under the 60
War Measures Act is one that I am sure will not appeal to the people of the West. What the people of the West want in this particular situation is a market for their low grade wheat.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: A permanent market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is not an absolute qualification.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: They both put forward the argument, "Under the War Measures Act you have taken off the duties, but those duties are merely suspended, and as soon as the war is over they will jump back again."

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is also what my hon. friend from St. John says.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That is what the law says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
But that is not what the Department of Justice says, and the Department of Justice is right. There has been presented to this House the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, a man who has absolutely no political reason for misstating the law or the facts, or for



coming to any particular conclusion as opposed to any other conclusion. He is there to advise Liberal Governments and Conservative Governments alike. He is a good counsel, a sound lawyer. And what does he say? He says, as any lawyer who looks at it from a legal standpoint would he bound to say: you have taken the duties off wheat, wheat flour and semolina, and those duties are permanently taken off until fresh duties are imposed by or under the authority of Parliament. That is what he advises the Government, and that is what the Government believes has been done.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Will the hon. minister undertake to say that the Deputy Minister of Justice expresses the opinion that the Government could not, by Order in Council, during the pendency of the war, transfer these articles hack to where they were before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
No, I do not.
Mr. 'PUGSLEY: How, then, does it become permanent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I will explain in a moment. Wheat, wheat flour and semolina are upon the free list in precisely the same sense as any other article is on the free list under the tariff to-day. Any article can be changed from the free list to the dutiable list toy or under the authority of Parliament.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister mean to say that any article can be changed from the free list to the dutiable list by Order in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend asks me that question, which embraces this particular case, I express my opinion that it can. But I will say this, speaking now on behalf of the Government, that the Government regard wheat, wheat flour and semolina as upon the free list in the same way that any other articles on the tariff are on the free list, and that fresh duties will not toe imposed except by Parliament. Why do I eliminate " or under the authority of Parliament?" For this reason: Under the general legislation, apart altogether from the War Measures Act-

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Why did not the hon. gentleman submit the proposition to Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have covered
that ground so fully that I thought even a child could understand it. The hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) must have been 
asleep, or else he was talking to the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) who is a charming companion. But I make the statement that the Government understands what has been done in the same sense that its legal adviser understands it, and I say that if these duties are ever reimposed it will toe by Parliament. Why do I say that? Under the general legislation the Governor in Council at any time can place upon the free list any article or commodity that is used in connection with Canadian manufactures. Further than that, the Government can at any time grant remission of the duty under the Audit Act in cases where duty has been paid on articles imported. It is not an unusual thing for a government to reduce a duty, or even to place an article upon the free list. It is not altogether unusual-though power in this respect is more seldom exercised for the Government to grant remission ;of duty on articles that have 'been imported. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), when, in power, remitted the duty on coal; and we remitted the duty on cement on one occasion, 'because there was a scarcity of cement in the West. It is not an unusual thing, I say, for the Governor in Council to reduce or remove duties. But it is an unprecedented thing, so far as I know to impose duties by Order in Council; and I have no hesitation in saying that this Government, or any Government that succeeds it, if it desires to impose fresh duties upon these articles, will bring the proposal down to Parliament and have it enacted into law in the usual way. So we need not worry ourselves about these legal disquisitions and arguments about the validity of the Government's action under the War Measures Act-that argument entirely disappears.	-	[DOT]
Let me summarize what I have said: In the first place, there has been no departure from the traditional fiscal policy of the Conservative party, which has meant so much for the prosperity of this country since 1879; the policy of Sir John Macdonald, the policy of Sir Leonard Tilley, the policy of the present leader of the Opposition down to 1911. In the second place, conclusions as to what should be done in this matter has been reached upon the merits at the time decisions were taken, and having regard tp the national interest. And when I speak of the national interest I repeat what I said in 1916, that no one can think of the national interest of Can-

ada without thinking of the interest of the three great prairie provinces.
Now, the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) put forth a fifth criticism. It is really as unfounded and as little worth as criticisms one, two, three and four. He says: You are actuated by political considerations. One would hardly suspect my hon. friend from Assiniboia of suggesting that anyone could be actuated by political considerations. It would surprise me to learn that such a thought has ever crossed my hon. friend's mind. He says there is a coming election. What coming election?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) merely interjects that. What have the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan to do with the question of free wheat?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Just as much as they
had to do with cement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
And they had
nothing to do with cement. But my hon. friend from Assiniboia said " election," he did not say " ejections."

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, and I meant the
Dominion elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Absolutely. That is what the hon. gentleman .meant. What does my hon. friend from South Renfrew say to that?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Assiniboia makes it stronger than I did, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: But he puts my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) in error.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Not at all. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) will tell you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Assiniboia said that we had acted for political reasons having regard to the "coming election." Now let me say this: the Prime Minister of this country is about to introduce a Bill into this House for the extension of Parliament. We on this side of the House do not believe there should be an election at this time. Should there be an election, who will be responsible for it? Is an election to be apprehended? Did the Government take this action under the War Measures Act by Teason of its expectation that there would be an election when, at the same time, it is about to bring down a Bill to extend the term of Parliament? 60J
What then, is the force, and weight, and validity of the argument of my hon. friend?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The ballot boxes were sent to England two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Oh, we have heard all about that.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question? My hon. friend has touched upon something that has nothing to do with the free wheat question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend touched upon it for two hours last week.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend says the Government is going to bring down a Bill for the extension of Parliament. I would ask if the Government intend to deal with that as with other Government measures and carry it through by virtue of the majority they have in this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is an old and experienced parliamentarian, and I am surprised at him asking a question like that. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister is also an old and experienced parliamentarian, and I believe that when he brings down a Bill to this House he will bring it down in such fashion that no fault can be found with his action. My hon. friend from Assiniboia says: You are very blameable, you are really censurable because your action has pleased the West. He spoke with a sob in his voice. He said: Your action has pleased the West. I have to admit frankly to my hon. friend from Assiniboia that the fact that the West is pleased pleases the Government and pleases me. I am glad the West is pleased. We are all glad the West is pleased, and we are glad not as politicians but as Canadians. For the last five years of continuous campaign I have been represented as the sponsor for the big interests. The impression has been sedulously and persistently created through the West that the Government is hostile to the people of the West.
I represent the interests in this House, all the interests in Canada, big and little, great and small, industrial, financial and agricultural. That is my conception of my duty. I have never favoured one interest at the expense of others, and if there is any interest in this country which I have favoured in this House, in the Cabinet, and in the councils of the Government, it has been the interest of agriculture. The people of the West and the people of the East are brothers; all the people of Canada are the children of Confederation. We have no

favourites. Any public man who is discharging his duty to the state regards the interest of every individual and every section of the country, and action is taken not in the interest of this section or of that section but in the national interest. That is the policy which we attempt to follow, and have attempted to follow, since our accession to power in 1911.
I desire to say, because this question has been raised, that this Government has done more for the West than all of the Governments that preceded it, and I am glad that we have. It is right that we should. Let me tell you some of the things that we have done. Our first action when we came into power was to enlarge the boundaries of Manitoba. We placed the finances of that province upon a sound basis, we increased her annual subsidy, because we wanted to place her on an equality with the other provinces of the west, by $600,000, and we paid over $2,000,000 of back subsidies. We enlarged the boundaries of Manitoba. It was a proper thing to do and we did it. What have we done for agriculture? My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) introduced a Bill into this House wherety $10,000,000 was set aside for agriculture in the East and agriculture in the West. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) introduced a Bill for the building of highways throughout Canada. That would have been a great boon to agriculture both East and West but the Senate threw out that Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You had better sit down then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have learned
in the course of my life that it is not always wise to follow the advice tendered by an opponent. My right hon. friend perhaps remembers the old Latin saying:	Timeo
Danaos et dona ferentes-I fear the Greeks when they come bearing gifts. When my right hon. friend makes a suggestion it does not necessarily follow that I am wise to carry it out. I have referred to a few of the measures which this Government has introduced. Take the banking legislation. We have amended the Bank Act repeatedly in order that the farmer may be able to pledge bis grain and may be able to hypothecate his cattle in order to get advances from the bank. We have continually kept before us the interests of the agricultural industry. Then, take the taxation measures introduced since this war broke out. They are very seldom talked about in this House, although they are criticised sometimes outside of this House by hon. gentlemen opposite. Let us see how our taxation has been raised for this war-$1,000,000 from the banks, taxation upon circulation; a few hundreds of thousands from trust companies, loan companies and insurance companies; taxation upon luxuries; business profits tax. There has been no discrimination against the farmers in our taxation measures to meet the expenditures of this war. I stated in my Budget la6t year that it would be my object to avoid direct taxation upon the income or effects or property of the farmer; Why did I say that-because I have repeatedly said in this House that agriculture is the very foundation of our national prosperity. When all goes well with agriculture, all goes well with every other class and industry in this country, and all goes well with finance. That is the reason why we have adopted the policy w'e have in raising revenue for the purpose of meeting the expenditure of the war. It is well for Canada that we should have diversified industries in both East and West. The National Policy is a policy that tends to

promote diversified industry throughout the length and breadth of Canada. It is not well that the East should be wholly industrial; it is not well that the West should be wholly agricultural. There will be boys raised upon farms in the West as well as the 'East, with a genius for mechanics, boys destined to be captains of industry. Should we not have a policy under which those boys can employ their genius at home, or must we lose them to the great republic to the south? There should be diverse industries in this country, and that is the reason why this Government is devoted to the fiscal policy which has been often enunciated in this House. The population of this country of ours is made up of various races and nationalities. It is a sparse population scattered over half a continent, a country as large as Europe. Tile policy of any Government should be to promote national unity in this country.

Now then, my hon. friend puts forward as a criticism of this Budget that it would please the people of the West. I say again, for myself and the Government, that if the people of the West are pleased with what has been done, they are not more pleased than we are that we have been able to do it for them.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) puts forward an amendment. He is not content with what has been done. He puts forward a useless, an unnecessary, a trivial amendment. Is it a genuine amendment? Or is it a political expedient destined to fail of its purpose? Well, we know what it is. My hon. friend from Assiniboia has no doubt as to the validity of wdiat has been done. I have enunciated the policy of the Government to-day, and there has been read to this House the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice as to the effect of our action under the War Measures * Act. Why does he put forward this needless amendment? He desires to embarrass the Government, he moves it on a resolution to go into Committee of Ways and Means. His amendment will not deceive the people of the
West for one moment, not for one moment. It suggests on its face a want of confidence in the Government. It reflects on our intentions, it asperses our motives, it casts unfounded doubt upon our action under the War Measures Act. It should, without hesitation, be voted down by this House.
Mr. GEO. E. McCRANEY (Saskatoon): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is entitled to the thanks of this House for introducing the amendment which is now under consideration, if only for the reason that it has brought from the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) a most important statement with regard to this great question, which he did not think it necessary to refer to in his original budget speech, and also for the very definite pledge which he gave to Parliament that there would be no new duties added except by an Act of this House. The Minister of Finance gave us many reasons why free wheat should not have been given before the present Order in Council was passed, and he entirely justified its passage at the present time. He says that he would not have done anything contrary to the national interest. No one would expect a finance minister, of this country, or any person in this Howse to declare that he would act contrary to the national interest. We agree with him that he is acting in accord with the national interest now. What we say to him i,s that the Government, in having delayed this relief for so long a time, was not acting in the national interest heretofore. If one reads over the Order in Council he finds that emphasis is laid upon the fact that this is to be a great relief with reference to the lower grades of wheat. That would always have been the case. That was one of the great reasons always urged in this House heretofore for free wheat. And it has been "with respect to the lower grades rather than to the higher grades that the farmer heretofore has been losing in great amount. The explanation which the Finance Minister gives as to the change of attitude from then to now matters little, but the conclusion of his Order in Council is very important. He advises the Government that it is desirable in the national interest that free access be obtained for our wheat in the markets of the United States. 1 heard my hon friend the Solicitor General the other day. In reading over his speech, it seems to me that he took other ground than that of the Finance Minister. He not only proved that free wheat would have been an evil before the Order in Council was passed, but he also proved that it is an

evil now. He laid great stress on public opinion in the West. I think that I am doing him full justice when I say that the conclusion that one would reach after reading over his speech is that there were no economic reasons which would justify the Government in having placed wheat on the free list, and that the reason which appealed to him most and which he put forward with all the force of which he is capable, is that it was a measure to conciliate the West, and that it was in the national interest, to have the West satisfied. When one decides to adopt a policy of which the economic effect is not certain, but in order to satisfy a public sentiment, whether economically sound or not, the inference is very clear that the reason is political; and one is reminded of the statement which the Solicitor General made only a short fourteen months ago that he thought that 90 per cent of the agitation for free wheat was political and that ten per cent was economically unsound. Apparently he holds that the ten per cent is still unsound and he has adopted the ninety per cent to himself. Why? The change was made in response to public sentiment in the West. As we read the war news we find that leaders of armies which have to make great retreats explain their withdrawal as a problem of strategy. They devastate the ground between the old lines and the new, and they claim to have entrapped the enemy and to have shortened their own line. So it is with this Government. Their retreat from the old position to the new is only strategy. They have given up some of their trenches; they have shortened their lines, but they have not saved themselves from defeat. There are more trenches to be taken, and victory will come to the forces which have driven them back. The battle of lower tariffs and freer trade is still going on and will come to a victorious conclusion.

The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) correctly interpreted the spiiit in which this measure has been put before the country. He accepted it as a temporary measure and held out the hope that the substitute for it in a short time would be a preference in the British market. We have had the announcement from London that there are to be Imperial preferences, and we have

also the statement of Mr. Bonar Law that foodstuffs are not to come within that preference. Agriculture, the growing of foodstuffs, is our basic industry, and the effect of Mr. Bonar Law's statement is that that great industry will have no preference. We do not feel badly about it; our farmers have never asked for a preference and I do not think they want it. They want free trade in that market as they want it in this. One wonders what class of product this country will manufacture that will have a tempting preference in the mother country. One wonders whether our people will be satisfied to abandon the newly-added market for our great products in the United States in order to obtain a market for our manufactured products in the Old country. When this Government wants to do something to mystify the public and to convince a portion of the community that they would not go as far as they actually do, they issue a proclamation under the War Measures Act. When they attempt to raise 50,000 men for home defence, and find that their Nationalist supporters do not want them to have conscription, they use the War Measures Act instead of the Militia Act. Their attitude with regard to free wheat is in much the same class. They are afraid of some of their eastern supporters, and they have not taken the strong stand that they might have taken by legislation; they prefer to give reasons which are only temporary in their character for the introduction of such important legislation. It matters very little to me whether the effect of this Order in Council ceases automatically at the end of the war. I accept the statement of the Minister of Finance that he at least will not repeal the provision of free wheat by Order in Council. I think it is most unfortunate, however, that the public are led to believe that there is hesitation on the part of the Government, and that the course they have adopted in the matter of free wheat, which should be in the line of a permanent principle, is of such a temporary character. One must recall the reasons which were given in the public press for opposing free wheat in order to see how completely those reasons are negatived by the Order in Council. Some of the objections were as follows:
It ships our raw products into another country, there to be manufactured, thus making our Canadian farmers, hewers of wood and drawers of water to the Americans.
It permits Washington to fix our tariff for us.

It will lead to the destruction of the reputation now held by our grain by enabling the Americans to mix it with their baser grades.
It will give the United States millers a supply of hard wheat, thus enabling them to chase Canadian flour out of the markets of the world.
It will deflect our grain to United States channels, to the ruin of our transcontinental systems.
It will destroy the Canadian mills.
It will encourage the Canadian farmer to continue wheat mining instead of going into mixed farming.
It will ruin the Canadian farmer by subjecting him to the competition not only of the United States farmer, but of the wheat raisers in the thirteen countries with which Canada has most favoured nation treaties.
It will prevent Canadian farmers from getting preferential treatment under the Chamberlain scheme.
And, Sir, all these reasons, so relied on two years ago by the Government, fall with the passage of the Order in Council conceding free wheat.
In the Budget speech, the Finance Minister placed before us a condition of things for which the public of Canada is to be very highly congratulated. We have an income of $232,000,000. The minister points out that our war debt arising out of the war alone has been increased to the extent of $600,000,000, and that the total is in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000,000. In addition to that, we have been able this year to appropriate $60,000,000 to war expenditure which would otherwise have been added to our national debt. A year ago the minister was able to announce an appropriation of $45,000,000 in the same way, making a total of $105,000,000 by which we have been able to reduce the war expenditure and save the public debt. That is to say, we have added to the debt $600,000,000; we have expended another $100,000,000, a total of $700,000,000, and of that amount of $700,000,000 we have paid on account only $100,000,000, in round figures.
The means which have been adopted by this Government to meet this most extraordinary expenditure are the increasing of the general tariff by 7i per cent, the lowering of the preference on British goods by 5 per cent, the imposition of the stamp duties and the business tax; and this year the minister announces in his Budget Speech a further addition to the Business Profits War Tax. The minister has pointed
out that there is no tax on luxuries, for one reason, namely because the great bulk of imports from France under our treaty with that country are in that class, and that it is necessary, in order to keep up the credit of France on this side of the water that nothing should be done to reduce those imports. One is reminded that while the Minister of Finance of this Government is so solicitous for the credit of France on this side of the water, in respect of luxuries which do us little or no good, the same Government has restricted from the mother country, which is more than our ally, importations of necessaries and not luxuries by the addition of a duty of 5 per cent, and has embarrassed the mother country in that way in the matter of exchange on this side of the water. The additions to taxation are largely out of wal profits. If we are carrying on the war with our best energy, we hope that these profits will soon come to an end; and when the war is over, we must turn to altogether new sources of income in order to reduce this tremendous debt. There is to be no income tax, so the minister says, and one of the strong reasons given is that so many people have bought war bonds and that those bonds are not taxable. Those war bonds have been purchased by some 35,000 or 40,000 citizens of Canada, a comparatively small number, and the tendency will be that the bonds of the small holders will get into the hands of the big holder, and thus the poorer part of our population will be paying interest to the more wealthy part; yet instead of taking more from the publio, the minister promises that he will borrow more.
Our men in France and Flanders are making tremendous sacrifices. One cannot read in the papers of to-day of their heroism and of the mutilation that is going on there, without thinking that we have neveT really appreciated what our men at the front axe doing. We speak about our volunteer system as though, when men were willing to go to fight, 5 p.m. they liked to go. I cannot imagine that any man of choice would go into the experiences and scenes that are occurring at the front at this moment. It is only because of the very highest sense of patriotism, of devotion to this Empire and to this country, and of faithfulness to principles that any man would expose himself to the danger of mutilation and death. Perhaps, if when the war began, we had a different conception of what it meant, we might have taken
