speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I do not often impose on the time of honourable members of this House, I feel that I may be permitted to offer to the Minister of Finance my most hearty congratulations on the very successful wartime Budget that he has been able to bring down at this time, being the third year -of Canada's participation in this great war. I also wish to express to the hon. gentleman my hearty congratulations on the success that attended his latest war loan, which, like the two former issues, was very largely over-subscribed. I am sure it must be very pleasant for the Minister of Finance to see the confidence that not only the people generally in this country have in him, but also the directors of our financial institutions and the citizens of the great republic to the south of us, who have invested so largely in these loans and helped to make them such a decided success. I am sure
that I voice the sentiments of the greater majority of the people of this country when I say that we hope and trust that the Minister of Finance may be spared his usual good health for a long time to come, to guide and direct the financial affairs of this country.
I am going to make a few remarks from the standpoint of the dairy farmer and to endeavour to reply to some of the questions advanced in this debate. I have no brief for the farmers of this country, but as four of the products of the farm of this particular section have been referred to in the discussion, I think it is my duty to-endeavour to place the matter in a proper light before those who dwell in our towns and cities. The four articles to which I refer are used in every household- mint, butter, cheese, and bacon. Upon these items the farmers of this section depend for their income at this season. I was amused at the remarks of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member- for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville). It seems to me that the dwellers in the cities do not fully understand the position of the farmer. They seem to believe that the farmer is producing these articles to which I have referred at about the same cost as in years gone by. But that is a very wrong conclusion to arrive at. The remarks made by the hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred on the subject of the high cost of living are likely to give what seems to me a very wrong impression. I think the only solution of this very vexing problem is to turn some of the consumers of this and other countries into producers. I gathered from the remarks of these hon. members that they thought that the farmers of this part of Canada were receiving altogether too much hard cash for the products of their dairies. I do not -agree with that view. The farmers of this country, as was stated by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) this afternoon, are the hardest working class we have, and I rejoice that they are coming into their just rights. If the farmers are prosperous to-day I congratulate them, and I also congratulate the Government that has made it possible for them tc be prosperous. Any country that has -agriculture as its basic industry i-s bound to be prosperous. That is why Canada enjoys so much prosperity at this time.
Some of the utterances in this debate would go to show that the dwellers in our cities have not yet grasped the true position of the farmers. What is the great need of the farmers of this section to-day? Is it

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It appeared on April
25, 1915. While I am on my feet I am going to take this opportunity to congratulate the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir

Robert Borden) and his colleagues on the success that they have achieved in their efforts to aid the Mother Country since the outbreak of this great world war. Let me say, Sir, that through those efforts they have succeeded in sending to the front a great army of young men, the flower of the manhood of this country, whose valorous deeds on the battle field have resulted in writing the word " Canada " high up on the scroll of honour among the nations of the world. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the brightest pages in the history of this war will be those that chronicle the achievements of our Canadian troops and let me say, Sir, that the record will be read with the greatest possible pleasure by Canadian posterity. It was nobly said by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) the other evening that Canadians knew how to live and that they had proven to the world that for the cause of freedom they knew how to die. In passing, Sir, I think it is only right that I should also pay my tribute of respect to the women of Canada for the efforts they have put forth. Let me say that the wives, the mothers, the daughters and the sisters and sweethearts of Canada are those on whose shoulders have rested the greatest possible responsibilities and anxieties, and only by the supreme patriotism which they have displayed have they made it possible for this Government to achieve what they^have accomplished. They have given freely of their best, Loth sons and daughters, and I read with great pleasure the other day that there is no better class of nurses doing service in the great armies of the Allies than those who have gone from our own Canadian shores. Our doctors also have done a noble and humane work, but, Mr. Speaker, I think at the present time, we are too close to this great war to fully realize or appreciate what our own Canadian boys have succeeded in doing.
Let me say that the immortal deeds of the men of the maple leaf, the men who are proud to call Canada their home, will be recorded by the historians of the future; and generations of Canadians yet unborn will read with noble pride these pages in the book of history. When this great ^.conflict has come to an end, When this cruel war is over, and when the dove of peace has again unfolded and spread her wings over the warring nations of Europe, then Canada will stand out pre-eminently among the nations of the world as the one nation that went into this fight, not from compulsion, but from a higher, loftier and

nobler motive, a sense of duty and a patriotism that would not be denied, to secure for all time to come justice and liberty for the smaller nations of the world.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we, the people of Canada, like all the citizens of the great British Empire to which we are so proud to belong, are fully resolved to face to a finish whatever the future may bring, until, in the providence of God and through the valour of our noble men, victory shall rest on our flag, and righteousness shall have been vindicated.
Mr. GEORGE W. ICYTE (Richmond, N.S.): Mr. Speaker, the intervention of the Minister of Finance in the Budget debate this afternoon for the second time would seem to indicate that something has happened to disturb the serenity which he usually displays in his addresses to this House. The papers of yesterday contain the statement that on Saturday last the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) delivered an address to his electors in the county of Victoria. In the course of that 'very interesting address he said:
In New York I was informed by a leading American financial magnate that I should not sail; that an attempt was about to be made to destroy me, and I was urged to cancel my trip. Thinking reference was had to torpedoes, I laughingly passed it off. The gentleman assured me, however, it was not torpedoes at sea, but "envenomed poison on the part of some of your own colleagues in the Cabinet who seek to get rid of the Prime Minister, but who realize that you are behind him solid, and in order to get rid of him they must first get rid of you."
The sequel to the statement of the ex-Minister of Militia is to be found in the presentation of the Finance Minister this afternoon. We remember that on Friday last the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) addressed this House upon the question of free wheat. There is apparently a feeling in this country supported by electors who are in sympathy with the Finance Minister that, should the conspiracy of which the ex-Minister of Militia speaks succeed, the Minister of Finance will be selected to lead the Conservative party. On the other hand, there are elector in the West supporting the Conservative party who believe that the honours and the mantle of the present Prime Minister should fall upon the youthful shoulders of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). I beg to assure the Finance Minister, that the speech made by the Solicitor General on Friday evening last did not at all require his intervention in this

debate. While the Solicitor General did the very best he could, I assure the Finance Minister that he did not enhance his reputation as a special pleader by the address which he delivered to the House as to the reasons why the Government granted free wheat under the Order in Council of the sixteenth of April. I may with equal confidence assure the Solicitor General that the speech made by the Finance Minister this afternoon did not put him in a light superior to the Solicitor General in special pleading as to a subject on which neither of them appear to .have much enthusiasm.
The Minister of Finance endeavoured to get some consolation out of the volte-face which he and his colleagues turned upon the subject of free wheat, from the traditional record of the Conservative party with respect to reciprocity. He pointed out that the principle of reciprocity was accepted by the Conservative party away back in 1878 and that he was not acting inconsistently with that policy in adopting the platform of free wheat as he did on a recent occasion. I might say that the resolution moved in the House of Commons by the Conservative party in 1879 in which the subject of reciprocity was mentioned, was formulated froih a platform that was intended only for the purpose of getting into power, and the moment the Conservative party got into power they spurned the policy of reciprocity. Only when they were driven by the force of public opinion to accept its tenets was it adopted as part of their policy. We remember that in 1891 the Conservative party, having regard to the growing sentiment in favour of reciprocity throughout Canada, and being then face to face with a Dominion election, thought it would be to their interest to catch the vote of the farmers of the 'Dominion of Canada by professing to be in favour of reciprocity. But the gentlemen who formulated that policy did not receive the sanction of the Government of the United States, notwithstanding that Sir Charles Tu.pper, the spokesman of the Conservative party on that occasion avowed in the midst of the campaign that it was unnecessary for the people of Canada to support the Liberal party in order to get reciprocity, that they themselves were negotiating an extended measure not confined to natural products alone, but embracing manufactured goods as well. We know that the Secretary of State in the United States Government of that day took an early opportunity to repudiate the statement made by Sir Charles Tupper, and since then the
Conservative party did not again venture to take up the subject under the name of reciprocity, notwithstanding that, in 1879, the policy of the party was adopted to bring about a reciprocity of tariffs and thereafter a reciprocity of trade. The speech of the Finance Minister this afternoon also accentuated the fact that he and the Solicitor General are not in accord as to the results which will flow from the placing of wheat on the free list. The Solicitor General, in his speech on Friday afternoon, said:-
Where are the hon. gentlemen who in this House year after year assured us that as soon as we let .down these iniquitous harriers the Winnipeg price would advance to the Minneapolis level to the benefit of the Canadian producer? If we follow the market after the 17th of April, we find that both markets advanced together with the same smaller spread between them that obtained the day before and the day after the Order in Council was passed.
The whole argument of the Solicitor General to this House on Friday last was that placing wheat upon the free list was of no advantage whatever to the western farmer, and he endeavoured to prove this by quoting figures.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I understood the Solicitor General to be referring to the higher grades, and x was speaking this afternoon with regard to the lower grades when I mentioned the payment of duty by the farmer.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The Solicitor General was referring to the price of wheat at Minneapolis. As I said, his whole argument was built up for the purpose of trying to convince the House that the placing of wheat on the free list would be of no advantage to the western farmer. He stated, further, that the only time when the placing of wheat on the free list might be of advantage would be when there was an export trade in wheat from the United States to Great Britain, but as there was no export trade at the present time, the result that the Liberals anticipated in the way of advantage to the farmers under an arrangement for free wheat could not possibly accrue to them now. If the placing of wheat upon the free list did not result in increasing the price of wheat to the Canadian farmer, it had the effect of immediately increasing the price of flour to the Canadian consumer. Immediately after it became known that wheat had been placed on the five list, flour took a jump of 30 cents, 50 cents and, in a few days, 75 cents a barrel. We can only argue from the observations made by the Solicitor General that at a time when the price

of wheat was low, when the farmers might reasonably accept a higher price to compensate them for their labours in respect of wheat-growing and when the price of flour was so moderate that the consumer could afford to pay a little more for his flour without feeling the burden of it, the present Government refused to put wheat upon the free list. But when abnormal conditions were brought about; when the placing of wheat upon the free list could not result in increasing the price to the farmer and would inevitably result in increasing the price of flour to the consumer, that was the time that the Government selected to place wheat upon the free list. The Finance Minister stated in the course of his speech that no industry in Canada has had greater profits since the outbreak of war than the milling industry; yet when the policy of free wheat was accepted by the Conservative party, the price of wheat for, the farmer did not increase, but the price of flour to the consumer did increase enormously. So that the consumer of Canada, after waiting for five years for the deliberate action of this Government to place wheat on the free list, is paying more for his flour than he ever did, and the farmer gets nothing in respect of the increased price of wheat.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman assume that that is the result of free flour?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It is not necessarily a result of free flour; it is the result of free wheat under the present conditions. It gave the speculator an opportunity again to boost the price of flour upon the pretext that because wheat was placed on the free list it was necessary to increase the price of flour. The Solicitor General has met that by saying that the putting of wlheat on the free list has not increased the price to the farmer so that'there is no justification for increasing the price of flour to the consumer.
The Minister of Finance endeavoured to convince this House that the placing of wheat upon the free list by Order in Council at this time could have had no relation to political conditions in Canada. The last time a change in the tariff was made, by this Government under Order in Council was in the year 1912, upon the eve of an election, in the province of Saskatchewan. It was the intention of the Government without previous intimation to reduce the price of cement, and an Order in Council was passed by this Government cutting the cement duty in two. That action synchronized with 
the holding of a provincial election in the province of Saskatchewan. If, therefore, at a time like this we on this side of the House find the Government by Order in Council again making appeals to the farmers of Western Canada in respect to the wheat, the hon. Finance Minister should not be angry with us if we associate his conduct in this respect with the election to be held in the province of Saskatchewan in the course of a few weeks.
The Finance Minister has taken great credit to ihimseu for the many good things which he has brought about on behalf of the farmer. I no not think it is the desire of any person on this side of the House to rob the Finance Minister of any credit or glory to which he is justly and properly entitled in respect of the effect of the policies of his department upon any of the interests of this country. He said among other things that in the interests of the farmers he had put through an amendment to the Banking Act which enabled the farmer to hypothecate his stock for the purpose of -securing loans. That was a condition which reflected not so much upon the fairness of the Finance Minister as upon the failure of the present Government to perpetuate the condition of affairs that existed when they came into office. It is true that the predecessor of my hon. friend, during the fifteen years that ihe was Minister of Finance, did not amend the Banking Act for the purpose of enabling the farmers to hypothecate their stock, because money being plentiful and farming operations profitable, it was not necessary in those days for the farmers to hypothecate their stock in order to raise money. But with the coming of the Conservative party into power a changed condition of affairs was brought about and it was neces-s-ary for the Finance Minister to give authority to the farmers to hypothecate their stock in order to obtain the -money necessary for their daily needs.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House rose at six o'clock I pointed out that the only result of placing wheat upon the free list on the 16th of April last was to increase the price of flour to the consumer, a price that had already reached such a height as to make it in many instances impossible for the working people throughout Canada to obtain for themselves and

their families the quantity of flour necessary for their support and sustenance. On the Montreal market, on the 17th day of April the price of flour had advanced 30 cents a barrel which meant a total advance of $1.40 in a week. Manitoba brands jumped 40 cents a barrel and Ontario brands jumped 60 cents a barrel by the 18th day of April. The cause of this rise in the price of flour is not the scarcity of wheat in Canada, because the market reports of that date informed the public that there was in Canada a surplus of 81,500,000 bushels of wheat. The export trade had ceased owing to the German submarines, and notwithstanding the fact that we had this large surplus of wheat in Canada, and notwithstanding the fact that the amount of the duty on wheat had been taken off by the Order in Council of the 16th of April, the price of flour continues to rise. The Financial Post, on the 17th of April had this to say:
Flour advanced twice during the week, a total increase of seventy cents a barrel, a record for flour, which brought the price up to $10.70. The highest figure for flour prior to this was $10.50 in November last. The export flour business fom Canada is practically at a standstill. The Ogilvie Flour Milling Company informs the Financial Post that space is not available for ordinary commercial business overseas. The high cost of living is a regrettable economic fact, over which the packers and canners and other distributors of foodstuffs have no control. The enormous and eager demand for our products has brought about the situation. The remedy, as far as the Canadian consumer - is concerned, is to reduce his demands.
During all this time, no effort was made on the part of the Department of Labour, that had particular charge of the question of prices under the proceedings which it had originated some months ago, to regu-iate the price of flour and other foodstuffs in Canada. The Minister of Finance stated this afternoon that the milling industry in Canada had made larger profits since the war began than any other industry. His statement is borne out by an announcement in regard to the Ogilvie Milling Company which was published in the month of October last, and which reads:
A bonus of 4 per cent, for the year ended August 31st last was declared by the directors of the Ogilvie Flour Mills Co., Limited, on its $2,500,000 common stock, at a meeting held here yesterday afternoon. The bonus will be paid on October 1st along with the regular quarterly dividend of 2 per cent., making a total distribution out of the year's profits of 12 per cent.
The bonus declared yesterday is the first extra distribution to be made by the Ogilvie Company since the stock was listed on the Montreal Exchange in 1908, although bonus payments have been popular with other milling concerns when an exceptionally good run of business has been struck. When the stock was listed the common shares were returning 7 per cent.; the rate was advanced to S per cent, in 1910 and has been held steady at that level through good times and bad.
A year ago, when exceptional profits from wheat brought the earnings up to the phenomenally high level of 95 per cent, on the common,-
That is apparently an error.
-the directors held to their conservative course, and shareholders received the usual 8 per cent and nothing more. Investment values added to by this conservation of resources have naturally been potent in increasing the earning power of the stock. The status of the company, with a large supply of liquid capital at its disposal, has changed from that of a borrower to a lender.
At yesterday's meeting the directors took the view that the results of another year's business having been extremely satisfactory, there was no reason why an extra distribution of profits should be withheld any longer.
So you will see, Sir, that the enormous prices that have been charged for foodstuffs are not due to the economic conditions brought about by the war, but rather to the advantage that has been taken of the war by the milling industry of this country to boost the prices at a time when the boosting of such prices might possibly be attributed to war conditions. I say again that the Department of Labour should have taken this condition of affairs into account and taken steps similar to those taken by other countries to prevent the undue enhancing of the prices of foodstuffs.
The Budget proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance do not indicate either courage or originality. It is the fourth Budget that has been presented to the House by the hon. gentleman since the war began. In the first session after the commencement of the conflict, the tariff was increased on certain lines, largely having reference to articles of household consumption, and again in the session 1915, another increase in the tariff was proposed by the Government and carried through this House. Last year, war taxes were levied upon the profits of certain manufacturers under conditions which have yielded to this Government the sum of $12,500,000. The Minister of Finance this afternoon took great credit to himself for adopting a system of taxation upon war profits; but the total amount of revenue obtained by

the Government from this source, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, is $12,500,000, whereas the increased revenue obtained by the Government by reason of the increased tariffs which were placed upon foodstuffs amounts to something in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000. So, while the manufacturing interests, those who are engaged in the manufacture of war materials, and whose business has improved by reason of war conditions and the increased price of monufacturers generally, have contributed to the revenue only $12,500,000, the consumers of Canada have contributed vastly more than that; and as a consequence we have the conditions that now exist in Canada in respect to the increased cost of living. It would appear that the monied interests in this country are still paramount. We know that in 1911 the issue in Canada between the two parties was whether there should be a Government in power whose policy was to reduce the tariff and thereby reduce the cost of living, or whether there should be a Government in power backed up by the interests that found it to their advantage to oppose the reciprocity pact and thereby maintain a continuation of high tariffs in Canada. The gentle manner in which the Minister of Finance has touched the manufacturing interests by war taxation goes to show that those interests are still in control of this Government, and that the welfare of the consuming population of Canada is a secondary consideration. During the last three or four years there has been an enormous increase in the acquisition of wealth by the manufacturing interests of Canada. No such corresponding advantage has accrued to our consuming masses or to the working men who have to depend on their day's pay for the support of their families. I have here a statement taken ' from a financial newspaper of the earnings of certain corporations in Canada during the last year which shows that the Dominion Bridge Company declared a dividend for the year of 16 per cent; Price Brothers, Limited, declared a dividend of 16.1 per cent, and in regard to the Dominion Textile Company, the Financial Post states that it hears that a bonus is on the cards for the shareholders of that company which is known to have had a successful year, the sales having reached the sum of $13,000,000. It says that the preferred stock will pay a dividend of 7 per cent and the common a dividend of 6 per cent. The profits of the Canadian Locomotive Company for the cur-
rent year amount to $700,000, being 35 per cent on common stock of $2,000,000, after paying $15,000 for preferred dividends.
Stanfield's Limited, after paying bond interest, sinking funds and contingencies, showed a profit of $109,688.83, equalling 141 per cent upon the preferred and capital stock of $750,000.
The net earnings of the St. Maurice Paper Company were $363,909 in 1'915, and $2,832,277 in 1916. The balance, after interest and depreciation were deducted, amounted to $1,582,792, equalling 15-8 per cent on the $10,000,000 stock outstanding.
The Union Bank Paper Company, which owns 75 per cent of the stock of the St. Maurice Company, had interest charges of but $187,000 per annum, and the depreciation charge of about $1,061,000 last year was exceedingly liberal. The Financial Post says that it is safe to assume that at least another 5 per cent or 6 per cent of actual stock profits is concealed in the 1916 depreciation charges.
The figures for Ames, Holden & McCready for the ten months of the fiscal year which will close on April 30, shows a very large increase in turnover over the previous year, and the profits will also show a very satisfactory gain.
Steel and Radiation Company: In 1914 their business amounted to $774,231.36, and profits $13,797.02; in 1915, business $342,344:81, and profits, $123,086.20, and in 1916, business $457,389.87, and profits, $303,601.33. It is stated that the actual earnings of the Company amounted to over 25 per cent.

The Belding-Paul-Corticelli Company, after allowing for preferred dividends for the year, it is understood can show a surplus equal to 10 per cent on the common stock. This will be equal to 15 per cent on the preferred, compared with 71 per cent in 1915 and 4-9 per cent in 1914.

With respect to the proposal brought down by the Department of Labour some few months ago on the subject of the cost of living, we have before us the Order in Council which was made public by the department, and on the strength of which the Minister of Labour claims credit for having done something calculated to reduce very materially the cost of foodstuffs to consumers. I will read a few sections from the Order in Council, showing the procedure to be followed. Section 3 says:
(1) No person shall accumulate or shall withhold from sale any necessary of life beyond an amount thereof reasonably required for the use or consumption of his household or for the ordinary purposes of his business.
(4) The Minister of Labour may, by notice in writing under his hand or that of his deputy, require any person who operates, controls or manages any cold storage plant, packing house, cannery, factory, mine, warehouse, or other premises in which or in any part of which any
necessary of life is prepared, manufactured, produced or held by such person for himself or for another, or who in any manner deals in any necessary of life, to make and render unto such minister precisely as required by him, a written return.
And the Order in Council states the particulars to be given in the return. Section 5 says:
Whenever the council or any municipality shall declare by way of resolution that in its opinion excessive prices are being demanded within the limits of such municipality for any necessary of life, such council may, by notice in writing under the hand of its clerk or other authorized officer, require any person dealing within the municipality in such necessary of life, and locally situate therein, to make and render unto such Council within a time set in such notice, and such person shall make and render unto such council, precisely as required by it, a written return under oath or affirmation.
And the Order in Council states the details, and then goes on:	*
If, after the receipt of any such return, such council shall consider that any circumstances justify reference of the return and a statement of the conditions to the Minister of Labour for further investigation at his hands, or if no return, or what the council shall consider an untrue or misleading return, is made, such council may, by way of resolution in writing expressing the facts and the council's conclusion therefrom report to such minister.
Section 6 says:
(1) If, after the receipt by the Minister of Labour of any return made to him or to any municipality in purported compliance with these regulations, such minister shall consider that any circumstances so justify, or if, after a return under these regulations has been required, none is made or none is made within the time set in the notice requiring such return or Within such further time as the Minister of Labour may upon special application to him allow, the said minister shall have power to investigate the business and to examine the premises, books, papers and records of the person making or failing to make such return, as the case may be, and, for those purposes such minister may appoint an Examiner or Examiners and may authorize in writing any examiner so appointed to enter and examine the premises, books, records and papers of such person, and to take evidence under oath or affirmation of any person who such examiner may believe has knowledge relating to such matters as ought to have been included within a proper return according to circumstances.
7. Whenever, in the opinion of the Minister of Labour, after an investigation and examination held in pursuance of the powers conferred by these regulations, an Tiffence against any of these regulations is disclosed: said minister shall remit to the Attorney General of any province within which such offence shall have been committed, for such action as such Attorney General may be pleased to institute because of the conditions appearing, certified copies of
(a)	any return or returns and resolutions of any municipality which may have been made, rendered or passed pursuant to these regulations and are in the possession of the minister



and relevant to such offence, and of (b) the evidence taken on any such investigation or examination and the report of the examiner.
8. (1) No prosecution for a contravention or non-observance of any provision of these regulations shall he commenced without the written leave of the Attorney General for the province in which the offence is alleged to have been committed, expressing whether such prosecution shall be by way of indictment or under Part XV of the Criminal Code.
If ever there was a gold brick handed out to the people of this country in respect to the investigation of prices and regulation of -the cost of living it is to be found in this Order in Council. Its effect is to provide that responsibility for action shall be transferred from the Government to the municipality, and from the municipality to the Attorneys General of the several provinces. There was a case in the city of Montreal where they attempted to define the procedure laid down in the Order in Council, but it was found absolutely unworkable.
I have here a statement made by the legal adviser of the city of Montreal, to the effect that the charging of high prices for commodities is not an offence under the terms of the Order in Council, and that the element of conspiracy must exist. This is given as the contention of the city law department in regard to the communication from the Minister of Labour:-
To speak only of the present case, it is established that certain coal merchants have made, all overhead and other expenses deducted, a net profit of $6 per ton. These facts have been disclosed to the Minister of Labour. He alone has the power to make further inquiry In order to ascertain if this coal was carried in excess of the reasonable quantity required for the business of each trader, or whether such increase would t>e different if such information was asked by an officer of the Department of Labour.
Here we have an instance of the practical working out of the Order in Council passed at the instance of the Minister of Labour with regard to matters in which that Order purported to give jurisdiction. But it appears that it is absolutely impossible for anything to be done under this Order in Council in the way of regulating the cost of living. Having issued the Order in Council, the minister feels that his duty is accomplished, and, notwithstanding that the prices of commodities which constitute the necessaries of life are going up by leaps and bounds without any valid reason, nothing is done to relieve the situation.

I do not wish to cumber Hansard with it. There is one point that has engaged the attention of the newspaper people of this country, and th<*t is the price of newsprint paper. For a year or more complaint has been made that the manufacturers of newsprint have been boosting prices far beyond what is called for by the conditions. They called the attention of the Minister of Finance to the matter some time ago, with the result that action has been taken. We on this side have contended that the Government ought to have adopted the policy applied by the Australian Government of fixing the prices of commodities which form the necessaries of life. Objection is raised that it would dislocate the course of business, and result in bringing about hardships instead of being advantageous to the public. With regard to the price of newsprint, the Financial Post of 17th April last states:-
The Financial Post understands that Sir Thomas White holds the belief that paper costs have advanced out of all proportion and is determined to enforce his views.
It is understood that any action taken would he along the lines of regulating the flow of exports by the placing of embargoes thus automatically reducing prices. '
But, instead of doing that, the Government adopted the procedure with regard to newsprint that we asked them to adopt with regard to food products. It is stated that an Order in Council gave authority to an officer of the Government to take possession of newsprint paper manufactured in this country fixing the selling price. As an agreement had been made between the manufacturers of newsprint and the Canadian publishers, fixing the price at $2.50 the order was not gazetted. This was the order which resulted in fixing the price of newsprint in Canada. But that order was not enforced, because the manufacturers climbed down and fixed prices satisfactory to the newspaper proprietors. The Grain Growers of the West are organized, and they were able to press their views upon the Minister of Finance, with the result that a few days ago wheat and wheat products were placed on the free list. The newspapers are an influential body of great public influence, and the Government was forced to take action in order that the grievances they complained of might be

relieved. But the poor consumer, the workingman, must worry along as best he can, with the cost of living increasing and his income not increasing in proportion.
Let us see what has been done in Australia with regard to the fixing of prices and regulating the cost of living. I have here the statute dealing with that subject. After providing for the appointment of a board, the statute enacts as follows:
6. (1) The Board and each Commissioner shall, in relation to any matter as to which it or he has power to furnish a report or make a recommendation under these regulations, have power to-

(3) If any member of the Board or any Commissioner or any other person authorized by the Board or by any Commissioner discloses, except in the course of his duty, or except to the Board ,or to the Commissioner as the case may be, any information obtained by him while upon any such premises, he shall be guilty of an offence.

Another section of the Act provides that any violation of the recommendations made by the commission shall constitute an offence and shall be punishable accordingly. Here is a Government that apparently is not afraid to take the full responsibility of dealing with this subject. The question of the cost of living was not any more pressing in Australia than it is in Canada but in Australia there is a Government that is in office for the purpose of governing in the interest of the whole community and not in the interest of a special class. I shall, before I am through, be able to show this House that the results of the statute passed in Australia has been to reduce the cost of living enormously as compared with the cost of living in the Dominion of Canada. The particulars, relative to the fixing of wholesale and retail prices of foodstuffs and necessary commodities and services in Australia, which appeared in Weekly Bulletin, No. 660, have caused a number of inquiries from Canada requesting more detailed information concerning the administration of the regulations and the results achieved.
Action in regard to the fixing of prices of foodstuffs and necessary commodities was taken by the Commonwealth Government under the War Precautions Act (1914-16). Regulations, known as the War Precautions (Prices) Regulations, were issued in July, 1916, to supersede price fixing measures which had been put into operation by some .of the state governments since the beginning of the war.
A commissioner has been appointed at the capital of each Australian state to administer the regulations and a Federal commissioner co-ordinates the work and is directly in touch with the minister in control of this section of commonwealth activity. The staff in each state consists of a commissioner, an inquiry officer and two clerical assistants. It is provided that a commissioner in any state may recommend that a certain article of fpod or any other goods be declared a foodstuff or necessary commodity under the prices regulations. On such item being approved it is proclaimed in the Commonwealth Gazette and inquiries are then undertaken by the commissioner in the state specially concerned, or in all states if the item is one affecting the interests of the whole Commonwealth.

The point in dispute between my hon. friend and myself is as to whether the dividend was earned or paid. I do not care whether it was paid or not; the statement says that the indicated earnings on preferred stock in 1916 was 24.31 per cent. Let us see how our friends would fare if they were doing business in Australia. If Stanfields Limited were doing business in Australia during last year, instead of contributing $14,297 to the public treasury, they would have contributed 50 per cent of their total earnings, or $54,844. If they were doing business in Australia in 1917, instead of contributing $14,297, as they will to this Government, they would
contribute to the Government of Australia the sum of $82,266. If the Consolidated Rubber Company were doing business in Australia, they would have contributed in 1916 to the treasury of Australia $453,750, compared with $154,687, which they paid here. If they were doing business in 1917 they would contribute to the treasury of Australia the sum of $680,625, instead of $247,500 that they are now paying. If the Dominion Canners Company Limited were doing business in Australia they would have contributed in the year 1916 $278,425, instead of $99,125 as they did, and if they were doing business in Australia they would tribute $417,637 to the treasury of Australia in 1917 instead of $177,120 which they will pay here.
The hon. Minister of Finance takes glory to himself for the amount of taxation that he has . levied upon the manufacturers of Canada. It would he well for him to look at what the Finance Minister of Australia is doing. The new war taxation brought down by the Finance Minister a few days ago is a viery complicated statement indeed. It is impossible for an ordinary man to figure out how much any company in Canada is liable to contribute, because the minister has graduated the percentages so that earnings up to a certain amount will pay 10 per cent up to a larger amount 25 per cent, above that 60 per cent, and so on to 75 per cent. That sounds very big, but when you come to figure out what it amounts to-I had this done by the Finance Department-you see how far short it falls, so far as contributions to the treasury are concerned, of the amount contributed in Australia. In that country the Government takes 50 per cent of the profits of every company during the first year and 75 per cent of the profits during the second year. There they have a government that watches the interests of the consumers. The prices of all the necessaries of life are fixed, with the result that the increase in the cost of living in Australia has only amounted to 9.4 per cent. In addition to that, the Government takes the profits of the manufacturers, so that they do not get any benefit or advantage out of the war that is not shared by the other people in that dominion. The consequence is that instead of a trifle of $12,500,000 being collected by the war tax upon manufactures, an enormous revenue is being collected from that source.
The Minister of Finance, as I stated in the early part of my address, did not show very much courage or originality in respect

of his taxation proposals. We have in Canada a tariff that has increased enormously the cost of everything to the consumer. Apart from the tariff existing before these war measures were brought down, there was an increase of 7$ per cent,
9 p.m. not only upon goods that were previously dutiable, but upon all free goods as well. The result has been to increase enormously the cost of living, whereas the Government have allowed the manufacturers to slip by with a very small proportion of taxation, considering the enormous profits that they are making. If the Finance Minister had adopted the principle of taxation in force in Australia and had exacted fifty per cent of the profits during the first year and 75 per cent during the second year, he would be able to put every article of consumption upon the free list and would have a larger income than he has at this time. If we are to have a happy and contented people; if we are to live under conditions that will enable us to bear the burdens of the war, the Government will have to get back to sound finance and economics. They must remove the duties upon the necessaries of life, as was done not only in France and Italy, but in Germany as well, and regulate the cost as is done in Australia. The consequence is that although these nations are very much nearer to the centre of war and suffer more grievously, under war cpnditions, than we do, they are not suffering in the matter of taxation nearly as much as we are.

DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The speculator has Taised the price of flour, and the Minister of Labour,
'Mr. Kyte.]
instead of dealing with the matter himself, has passed the puck on to the city councils and the town councils throughout the Dominion of Canada, and feels that he has discharged his duty by doing so.
It is not only in the matter of foodstuffs that we are' suffering; we are suffering in the increased cost of boots and shoes, clothing, rubbers, fishing supplies. Stanfields, Limited, for instance, are reaping the benefit of the enormous protection that it is receiving. The price of underclothing has been increased enormously to the consumers in this country, and, notwithstanding the payment of the war tax, the shareholders of Stanfields, Limited, are making more money now than they ever before made in their lives. We have in this country a condition of affairs approximating the conditions that exist in countries that are actually at war. Although we are a producing, a farming country, although the opportunities for transporting our produce to the other side to remedy the conditions of scarcity in Britain are unavailable to us and v>e have millions of bushels of wheat in this country, we are suffering the same exactions and privations that we would suffer if we were actually in a state of war. The Government felt that the only means of meeting the difficulties of raising revenue was by applying the system of taxation. It is extraordinary how our friends in the Conservative party, while they always preach that we should give and should make sacrifices, in the operations of Government and in the carrying on of their trade policy, take very good care that no sacrifices shall be made by their friends the manufacturers, who support them so loyally in this House and in the country.
Another source of complaint in respect of the administration of the affairs of Canada is the enormous expenditure of money which is being carried on at a time when war economy ought to be practised, while war economy is being preached by the Minister of Finance and by his colleagues in the Government. It is just about a year ago that we had in this House a discussion about a matter which indicated the wasteful methods in force in respect of the expenditure of money for the carrying on of this war. It is about a year ago, I think, that the question of the fuse contracts was discussed in this House and was referred to a Royal Commission. I am not going to discuss the findings of that commission, but it was found that every allegation made re-

garding the extravagant prices which were paid to friends of the Government was absolutely proved from start to finish, the result being that millions of dollars were lost to the taxpayers of this country. Allison, Yoakum, Lignanti are three names that w'ere familiar to us in Canada a year ago; not only were their names familiar, but their persons and physiognomies were familiar to the residents of the city of Ottawa. We do not see J. Wesley Allison around here as we did in those days nor do we see Yoakum and Lienanti anv more. What an autocry was raised against Liberals in this House because they dared to make allegations which resulted in the findings of the Royal Commission ! My poor, humble self was singled out as a person who ought not to be at large and who should suffer dire penalties. Poor, old .somnolent toryism! It forgets that the battle for free speech had been fought in Great Britain three hundred years ago and the victory won at the cost of a King's head. I am sure that my friends opposite regret very much that conditions exist in this country that permit free speech and free discussion. I state emphatically that the Opposition sitting in this House would not be discharging its full duty if it did not bring to the attention of the Government and of the country the shortcomings and maladministration of this Government in respect of war measures andi war expenditures. What is the remedy for the condition of affairs that exists at the present time?
We have had -some discussion in regard to changes and amendments to the tariff in order to meet the present conditions in Canada. For my part, our friends in the West cannot go too far in the matter of demanding reduced taxation and lower tariffs in this country for me to follow them. Every statement and every principle that have been enunciated on this side of the House with regard to tariff and the desirability of reducing tariff and reducing the cost of living will receive hearty and enthusiastic support from me. At the present time we have sources of revenue that are quite available to the Minister of Finance and quite adequate to all the demands notwithstanding that the demands aTe very great. As I pointed out a moment ago, if the minister only had the courage to adopt the system of taxing companies that exists in Australia, he could put all the foodstuffs and the necessaries of life upon the free list and still have more than enough revenue to meet all the actual requirements of the present time. After the war, there
will be great burdens to bear, and great courage required on the part of the Minister of Finance of the day. There is one field of taxation which has not been touched yet, and which the Minister of Finance seems to be afraid to touch. I refer to the taxation of income. By reason of the war we shall have in Canada a large number of millionaires who have become millionaires on account of the opportunity given them of making enormous exactions, not only through manufacture of war material, but through the manufacture of the necessaries of life. These manufacturers would never have received their millions out of the taxpayers, had it not been for the unfair conditions that have prevailed during the carrying on of the war. There is no more promising field of taxation to meet the requirements that will have to be met after the war than to make these gentlemen contribute of the millions that they have been able to acquire, while the common people of this country have been driven to the last extreme to meet the requirements existing in their households from day to day, and. while by far the largest proportion of them: have to mourn the loss of brave sons who have fallen in the field of battle.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget speech of the Minister of Finance contained two outstanding statements, one being that the debt of this country, which before the war was $336,000,000, had increased now to $900,000,000, and that before the end of the fiscal year it would be $1,200,000,000. For making identically the same statement, or perhaps even a more moderate statement, to their electors, some of my friends on this side of the House have been accused of disloyalty.
Another outstanding statement in the Budget speech of the Minister of Finance was that no tariff changes were proposed this year. Previous speakers have congratulated the Finance Minister upon the brevity of his Budget sipeech. Apparently, he has gone from one extreme to the other. Six years ago he was talking too much of a sort on the tariff question, hut to-day he avoids the tariff as he would a pestilence. Less than a year ago, only six months ago, in fact, when the western farmer was still marketing his crops, our Conservative friends were still strong in the faith that it would be of no benefit to the farmer to have the United States market open for his wheat. It would ruin the Canadian milling industry, they said, and would be very injurious to the dairying interests in Canada.

empty bags brought in. But what is the condition with regard to bran? The Finance Minister lays great stress upon the fact that our wheat crop was pooled with our Ally, the United States, and that we must do all we can to provide bread at reasonable prices. But man cannot live by bread alone-he must have butter on his bread. And how is this Government going to help the Canadian dairymen to produce more butter and more cheese and to answer the demands of the cities for cheaper milk and cream, when it places a tax of 25 per cent on bran and sorts coming into Canada? Let me show the Minister of Finance how that works out. Tine Order in Council enacting free wheat was passed on the 16th April. On the 14th April the price of bran in Buffalo was $43.50 a ton; in Toronto, $38 to $40, and in Montreal the same. .After this Order in Council has been in force for fourteen days, the price of bran had advanced for the Canadian dairyman to $43 to $45 a ton in Toronto, and the same in Montreal; but in Buffalo the price remains about the same as it was on April 14 (indeed a little less), prices being quoted at from $43.75 to $43.25, with $42.25 for May delivery. Thus there is no advance in the price of bran in the .United States, but an advance of $5 a ton in Canada. How does the Finance Minister think the Canadian farmer is going to answer the appeal for more butter and cheese, and cheaper milk and cream, under these conditions? But the position is even worse than that. We read in the trade journals of Montreal that last week hundreds of carloads of bran were sold for immediate or future shipment to the United States. It will not be long until there is more and cheaper bran in the United States than in Canada. You cannot blame the miller if he ships his-bran to the highest market, but if the Canadian farmer wishes to import bran from the United States he is met by a tariff created by this Government. Bran at Buffalo worth $43.25 per ton is subjected to a duty of $10.80 a ton coming into Canada. That is equal to $216, per car load. But supposing that bran dropped to $30 per ton, as bran is likely to come down as the grass gets better, the duty will be $7.50 per ton coming into Canada, or, in other words, the Government will be collecting from the farmer on every carload of bran that he brings into this country $150. Supposing bran again drops to $20 per ton the duty will be $5 per ton or $100 per car load. In other words, for every car load of bran, made from Canadian wheat milled in the 
United States, that the Canadian farmer brings into Canada, the Government demands one of his best cows.
My hob. friend from Brockville '(Mr. Webster) this afternoon pointed out that the price of live stock was almost double what it was five years ago. He gave as the reason that the farmers could not raise live stock profitably if they shipped their milk and cream. I would like to show my hon. friends how they 'are responsible for this condition. Had we accepted the reciprocity proposal we would have had a market for our butter and cheese in the United States. But we turned that down. The United States revised their tariff and placed milk and cream on the free list. The immediate result of that change was that, from all the eastern townships and from parts of Ontario where they could ship, carloads of milk and cream were going into the United States. Where they could not ship the milk and cream they shipped the cow. Canada lost not only the milk and cream, the butter and cheese, but the profit on the cow, and the labour that might have been utilized on Canadian farms and in Canadian factories manufacturing Canadian cream into butter and cheese to be exported as butter and cheese. The result of this condition is set forth in a bulletin prepared by Mr. Grisdale of the Experimental Farm. Hon. gentlemen can find it in sessional papers No. 16, of the year 1917. In 1913, the year the United States revised their tariff, Mr. Grisdale says that there were 2,188,824 milk cows in eastern Canada. In 1915, after two years of this policy, under which our milk and cream were going to the United States, and under which butter and cheese were prohibited, the milk cows of eastern Canada had decreased in number by 113,074. But it was worse with young cattle. Mr. Grisdale says that in eastern Canada, in 1913, there were 2,479,406 cattle other than milk cows. Two years later the number had decreased by 603,902. That is a condition that has been brought about by changes in the United States tariff. I would plead with the Minister of Finance; just now we have a demand from the housewives of Canada for the admission of oleomargarine, for anything at all to get cheaper fat stuffs for the bread of the children. We have a demand from the cities for cheaper milk and butter. The farmer is blamed for advancing prices. The Finance Minister answers that demand by compelling the Canadian farmer to pay in his own market $5 more for a ton and $100 more for a carload of bran than he was paying fourteen days ago. He has placed

the further restriction upon the Canadian farmer that if he imports bran from the United States under the present conditions he is met at the custom house with a price of $216 per car loa4. The Minister of Finance boasted this afternoon-and I am just as proud as he is that I am a farmer's 'boy. He was proud to have been on the farm. I know that the Minister of Finance knows something about farming, probably more than our western farmers do. Farming in the West, after all, is not a very strenuous occupation. The man puts in his crop and waits for it to ripen, then he harvests it, markets it, and he is through. But, in eastern Canada, where men milk and provide milk, cream, butter and cheese for the cities, farming is altogether another proposition. Where a man on the farm has to rise on a cold winter morning and go out to the stable with a coal oil lantern it is a slavish job all the way through, and under these circumstances how can the Minister of Finance expect that the farmers are to increase their herds of milk cattle when the Government creates conditions that make it more expensive for them to produce? I hope the minister will change his mind, and that before we get through with the session he will introduce such legislation as will enable our Canadian farmers to get their bran and shorts without being compelled to go to the custom house and pay an increased tax.
This is a time when we all admit that we have made mistakes. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Sevigny) openly acknowledges that he made a mistake in 1911. The M'hiister of Finance himself has acknowledged that he made a mistake in opposing tariff concessions in 1911. He has made that acknowledgment by an Order in Council. Statesmen from overseas are in Washington in order that by consultation and advice our new Allies may avoid the mistakes made by us in earlier days. Our own veteran statesmen, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is at Washington and the newspapers tell us that the Minister of Finance and my hon. friend and former fellow-citizen the Minister of Inland Revenue are also to go to Washington. Why not take advantage of the occasion to say to our neighbours that in 1911 we were wrong when we declined to accept their fair trade with them? Let us have a fair trade that will be satisfactory to the East and the West. Will the Minister of Finance rise to the occa-them? Let us have a fair trade that will be conditions which will satisfy the East and
the West and prepare the road for a growth and extension which we all hope for Canada, or will the Minister of Finance leave that to his successors? That is a question I am not able to answer.
If I were looking to my own interest and that alone, I would not object too strongly to this protection on bran and shorts. But I am not elected to this Parliament of Canada to look after my own business. I am elected to look after the dairymen of the constituency which I represent, and I beg to submit an amendmeht to bring the matter fairly before the House. I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Kay (Missisquoi) as an amendment to the amendment:
That to ensure a plentiful supply of bran, shorts, and middlings for the farmers to produce millc, cream, butter and cheese, and for the raising and fattening of livestock, this House is of the opinion that wheat, bran, shorts, and middlings should, without delay, be placed, on the free list.
