subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to ask the attention of the House for a few minutes I certainly do not intend to delay the House at any great length. I have not been in the habit of taking up much of the attention of this House while I have been a member, and I suppose that it is but right that I should occupy one of the back benches. But, Mr. Speaker, representing as I do an agricultural district, I feel that it is. my duty to extend to our Minister of Finance the congratulations of the agriculturists of my county, not only those of my county but the agriculturists and, in fact, the whole people of Canada, on the manner in which he has handled the financial affairs of this country. Without going back to the Budgets of the past, let us take simply the one that is before the House to-day.
But before going any further, I feel that I should reply to one statement that the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) made in his opening remarks, when he referred to the men on this side of the House as allies of the Nationalist party. I would aAk him to look to his friend the member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) if he wants to know what a Nationalist is.

The hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have accused us of an alliance with the Nationalist party. They accuse these men here of being Nationalists. They deny them the right of reformation. But let him look to his friends on the other side of the House for the last two years who have been preaching the doctrines of the Nationalist party, and no man knows it better than my hon. friend the member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). He has seen the evidence of it right in the village of St. Remi where the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville had as his principal orators Armand Lavergne and Tancrede Marsil. Let him look into the history of the Nationalists of this country, let him look into the history of the men who have been preaching treason, nothing short of treason, gentlemen, and he sits there, the man who had two of those men as his chief speakers. Then they accuse the Conservative party of connection With the Nationalists. Shame, I say, on hon. gentlemen opposite. If anything, let us be honest. If we are wrong we will admit it. There are men sitting on the Conservative side who have admitted that they did entertain principles favourable or in keeping with the Nationalist principles. They have seen the folly of their ways and have reformed and to-day they are accused by men on the opposite side of the House because they did reform. I would ask hon. gentlemen if Jesus Christ accused St. Paul for reforming? St. Paul was a persecutor of Christ at one time. Did you or any man ever hear of Christ accusing St. Paul for having reformed? Oh, woe unto ye scribes and hypocrites.
I had no intention of launching into a discussion of that sort when I rose to speak. I rose in the first place to congratulate our Minister of Finance, not only the Minister of Finance but the whole Government, on what they have accomplished within the last five years. I think that I have the people of Canada hack of me when I make the statement that without going back to former Budgets, the Budget that is to-day under discussion has the approbation of ninety per cent of the honest people of Canada, regardless of the criticism that you hear from the opposite side of the House; for we know, and we can fully realize by the nature of the criticism that has come from the opposite side of the House, that the hon. gentlemen opposite are not sincere and consequently are not honest in their criticism. We can have no better illustra-
tion of it than in regard to the matter of free wheat. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been clamouring for that for a number of years.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Now they have got it, and yet the criticism of the Government to-day is stronger than ever it was before, which leads me to believe that for political purposes hon. gentlemen opposite would deprive their people of what they have been clamouring for for a number of years. We can only judge of that by the statements they have made in the House. I feel justified in saying that the great majority of the people of Canada to-day are satisfied and are offering their congratulations to our Minister of Finance on the manner in which he has handled the financial affairs of Canada. I have no intention of going into details of our national finances. That has already ben done so thoroughly, and the situation has been so well elucidated by the minister himself and by the Solicitor General, that it would be folly on my part to attempt to delve into it. Besides that the financial situation to-day has developed into such tremendous proportions that I am free to admit that it is baffling to the ordinary mind. But we feel to-day that in the man who has charge of the finances of this country we have a master of finance. Future history will record him as such. Not only can I say this of our Minister of Finance, but if I had time I might go over all of the departments and point with pride to their administration.
I will simply gii*e the house a few impressions. Next to the work that has been accomplished in connection with the finances of Canada is that which has been accomplished by the ex-Minister of Militia. I feel satisfied, Sir, that when the history of this country shall he written, the name of Sir Sam Hughes will go down to posterity as one of the greatest men of Canada, notwithstanding the vile attacks that have been made by some hon. gentlemen opposite upon his character. They did not dare to come out openly with any statement, but by certain charges that were made or insinuated, they attempted to cast slurs on his name. But the attempt was an absolute failure, and the verdict of the people to-day is that the charges which were made in this House last winter were without foundation and were brought forward purely for political purposes.
Mr.' TURRIFF:	Why did the Government kick him out, then?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The Government are not kicking. They are going to make hon. gentlemen opposite kick 'before they get through with them. As the representative of an agricultural district, I should not fail to make mention of the Department of Agriculture. I feel sure that I shall be backed by 90 per cent of the people whom I represent when I say that the present Government has done more for agriculture than ever has been done in our district in the past, particularly in connection with the live stock industry. I shall not attempt to go into the details of the work of the Department of Agriculture, which is better known perhaps, ito other members of the House than it is to me. One branch that I wish especially tp call attention to is the Live Stock Branch, particularly the distribution of male animals, which had its origin in the mind of our late friend, John Bright, who was the head of that branch of the department. En passant, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that it would be out of place if I were to say a word with regard t,o the death of our friend John Bright, who, I feel, is lamented by agriculturists from one end of the land to the other. He has, perhaps, done more for that particular branch of the department than any other man living. There originated in the mind of John Bright things that never were done in Canada before. He was attentive to his duty, courteous to any one who met him and ready to give good advice and counsel to any one who went to see him. I feel that Canada, and particularly the Department of Agriculture, has met with a great loss in the death of John Bright.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: We have heard a great deal about free wheat. I was somewhat surprised to hear the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) criticise that measure. Like many of his friends in the past, he has agitated in favour of free wheat. In rejecting that measure the Government did perfectly right, and under former conditions I am pleased to say that this measure is not a change of policy; it is simply an emergency measure consistent with the trade policy always followed.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It was done to meet the extraordinary conditions that have been brought about by the submarine warfare.
I am glad that we have a Government that is large enough and broad enough in mind
to meet ^situations of that kind. I would myself prefer that this be not a permanent policy, because I do not believe that free wheat would eventually be a benefit to the farmers of the West. Moreover, in legislating here we must have Tegard to the farmers of the East. The member for Huntingdon knows as well as I do that the stock men of the East are dependent, in a large measure, on the by-products of wheat. If we send our wheat to the United States we shall be deprived ^f that by-product, and, as a matter of fact, do injury to the stock men of the East by granting free wheat to the farmers of the West.
I have listened with a great deal of attention to the speeches delivered by the hon. gentlemen opposite. I have no doulbt that had these same gentlemen gone before the country when the agitation for the Transcontinental railway was in progress they would not have dared to make the statements that they have made in the House to-day. The principal argument made at that time was the necessity of transportation for the great products of our western country-the transportation of our manufactured products from the East, and of the products of the great prairies from the West. That was a reasonable argument, and the people accepted it, the Transcontinental railway was built upon that ground. These same gentlemen now tell us that we should deprive this road of the benefit which would accrue to it through the transportation of the products of the West, by diverting those products to the south. I have been a Rrotect-
10 p.m. ionist all my life, and, my belief in the principle of protectionism is stronger to-day than ever it was. Before hon. gentlemen opposite took office in 1896, the great dividing line between the two parties was protection or free trade. Hon. gentlemen opposite advocated free trade, although possibly they were not all out-and-out free traders. Just as soon, however, as they came into power, they swallowed with one great gulp all their free trade talk and they simply had to come down from their perch and accept the Conservative policy of protection. That fact is well known to the people of Canada, regardless of what hon. gentlemen opposite may say. If one talks with the thinking men of this country, one will soon realize that. There are a few things that come home forcibly (to jthe ordinary man, and I will cite only two of the reasons why I am in favour of protection. In the first place, it cannot be denied that this country of ours has prospered greatly under a protective policy; second-

ly, we have only to look to the Republic to the south of us to see that it has grown to be a great nation under one of the highest protective tariffs in existence. These are evidences that cannot be denied,
I' care not what arguments may be brought forward. They are facts going down in history and they cannot be gainsaid. It is said that Great Britain has prospered under a policy of free trade, but conditions there are absolutely different to-day from what they were when Great Britain was in the process of establishing her manufacturing industries. We are told that during the Spanish war the workmen of Great Britain learned from the people of Spain-the methods of manufacturing fine fabrics, and that when the Spanish war was over, they came home and put into operation what they had learned in Spain. Great Britain thus grew with practically no opposition until it became the greatest manufacturing nation in the world. When my hon. friends opposite seek to cast reflections upon the manufacturers, they are making a great mistake. We require the agriculturists, but we also require the manufacturers to consume what the farmer produces, and we have that illustration in Great Britain which has become, if not the greatest, one of the greatest nations that the world has ever known, and that result has come about principally through her vast manufacturing industries. Circumstances change, however, and Great Britain now realizes that she has made a mistake in recent years in not putting on a protective tariff. We can see now that Germany had made inroads into the trade of Great Britain and of all her overseas Dominions. Right in our own country we have seen the inroads that the Germans had made in selling to us products that we could manufacture ourselves, and that I think we shall manufacture in the future. That goes to show that a protective policy is the only proper policy for a young country such as Canada.
Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite as well as hon. gentlemen on this side of the House feel that I am in rather a happy frame of mind, and I may say that I am in so far as this Government is concerned, because as a supporter of this Government I do not think that we have anything to fear in appealing to the country. Although no man in this House or in the Dominion would regret more than I would a general election at the present time when our country is at death's grip with an enemy, yet I feel sat-
isfied that with the record that this Government has at its back, we can go to the country with confidence. I would feel sorry for. a man who endeavours to force an election on this country at the present time because I know that that is contrary to the wishes of the people of Canada regardless of their politics. Some of the most staunch Liberals in my constituency are absolutely opposed to an election at this time. The hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) notwithstanding the efforts he has been making during the past year when he has absolutely violated the truce, knows that the people , of his own constituency do not approve him; he knows that the Liberal catechism of his own county, the Huntingdon Gleaner, condemns the action that he has taken during the last two years. Later on, Sir, I may have occasion to refer to those matters, but for the present nous avons fini.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not purpose answering the charge of dishonesty. We on this side of the House occasionally have charges of disloyalty and of want of patriotism hurled at us, and my hon. friend (Mr. Morris) in the desire to make a few more charges against us, charges us with being untruthful, insincere, etc. We are quite willing to let those charges go for what they are worth. I would like, however, while the Minister of Finance is in his seat, to refer to one remark of my hon. friend. I was unfortunately absent when the minister was speaking this afternoon, but I understand that he said that the Order in Council providing for free wheat would not be repealed except by the authority of this House, while the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Morris) says that it is merely a temporary war measure and not a policy at a11 I must say that the remarks of the Solicitor General are open to the same construction as the remarks of the last speaker. If I am correctly informed, the remarks of the Minister of Finance, however, are not on the same line.. I am advised that be said this was a permanent policy until repealed by the House. I will leave the last speaker and the Solicitor General and the Minister of Finance to settle these things amongst themselves. We can take whatever meaning we like out of the speeches, and I suppose that was their intention. If we want to believe it is a permanent policy, we can. believe it; if we want to believe it is a temporary policy, we can believe that, and so on. No doubt

these opinions are given out to satisfy different sections of public opinion.
A short time ago I read an address delivered by the Minister of Finance at St. James Methodist Church, Montreal. He disclaimed any intention of preaching a sermon, but I think myself it was rather a good sermon that he delivered on that occasion. His subject was, Self Denial and Self Sacrifice; a very good subject to preach on whether in a church or in this House, and it struck me it would not be a bad text for the minister to dilate upon before his special friends, the highly-protected interests of Canada; I think an address of that kind is very much needed in that quarter. The Minister of Finance, it seems to me, might equally well have called his subject *' Efficiency.*' Among other things he said at that meeting:
Increased production is necessary, increased agricultural production especially. Every acre, every plot of land in the Empire, should be made to produce this year to the utmost of the human energy available for the purpose.
Further on he says:
It is the bounden duty of every citizen to multiply his efforts to greatly increase production.
The minister is right. Increased production of foodstuffs for the Allies is sorely needed, and Mr. Balfour eeems to have impressed, this need upon the people of the United States. But in order to secure this increased production there must be increased efforts and increased efficiency. There are difficulties, however, in the way of increased production in this country. Speaking of the particular part of the country with which I am best acquainted, we have many difficulties to contend with. We have had two bad threshing seasons followed by two late springs, which have greatly curtailed spring and fall ploughing, and necesarily curtailed also the production of food stuffs. These difficulties, unfortunately, have at the same time increased the danger of a luxurious growth of the farmer's great enemy, the weed crop. Those however are not the only difficulties with which the food producers of our country have to contend. Some difficulties cannot be avoided, but others can. One of the great difficulties with which the farmer has to contend i6 the increased price he has to pay for his implements, caused by the high protective tariff imposed by this Government. In my part of the country the threshing season is very short, lasting only a few weeks. We are obliged to thresh out of the stook, because 62
it is impossible to ge the labour to stack. The result is that any man who has very much of a crop is obliged to have a threshing outfit of his own, not the very largest obtainable, but one that will cost him about $2,500. The most up-to-date outfits cost from $5,000 to $6,000, but the ordinary farmer would get one for his own use costing about $2,500. The duty the dealer would pay on that machine would amount to about $500. The dealer would undoubtedly charge the farmer something additional on the duty 'he was obliged to pay, let us say ten per cent on the $500; that would be $50, making $550 duty which the farmer would have to pay. Anyone who was asked to pay a direct tax of $550 for some article needed in his business would think it a tremendous charge, but it is only one of the many indirect taxes that we have to pay on account of our protective policy. If the threshing machine that was bought by the farmer was manufactured in the United States $500 of the amount paid by him would go into the treasury of this country; we are not grumbling about that. If the machine is bought from a Canadian manufacturer, the price would be just the same, if not a little more. But if the machine is bought from a Canadian manufacturer no part of the $500 duty that the farmer would otherwise pay would go into the treasury of this country; it would all go into the pocket of the Canadian manufacturer. Now, I find that in the last year for which we have official figures for the manufactures of Canada, we manufactured four times as much as we. imported. If that is true with regard to threshing machines, in order for the treasury of this country to collect $500 duty we should have to pay duty on five machines, one imported and four manufactured. I ask you if that is good business. It is an indirect tax it is true, but we have to pay it just the same as if it were a direct tax. The same remark applies to seed drills and a great many other farm implements. Self-sacrifice is needed not only on the part of the farmers, but on the part of the manufacturers as well. Our farmers were criticised for refusing an offer to sell their wheat to the Allies at a price less than one half the market price, and were even looked upon as disloyal by some. But we have got accustomed to this cry of disloyalty and want of patriotism. Only a few days ago an hon. gentleman on this side of the House who has a son at the front, and was anxious to see that he was not exposed to unneces-



sary temptation from the wet canteen, was told that he was unpatriotic for bringing up the subject in the House. Now, I think it would be a great deal better if we cut out these charges of disloyalty and want of patriotism. Many of us have sons at the front and may hear of their death at any moment, and if ever there was a time when this cry should not be raised, surely it is now. I would not like to charge any man with disloyalty, not even those political colonels who strut around our country in the King's uniform, drawing big pay, and who have been on a free trip across the Atlantic to England or France, but who, the moment they smelt gunpowder, turned tail and skipped back home, leaving their men to go to the front without them. I would not charge even these men with disloyalty, though it would be far more reasonable to do so than to make the same charge against our farmers. Sacrifice is needed not only from our farmers, but on the part of our manufacturers as well. There have been cases of self-sacrifice on the part of manufacturers in Canada, but these have been isolated cases, and we want it to be a general thing. The duties on the farmer's tools of trade, if I may call them so, should be absolutely taken off, and the customs duties reduced on other things required by the consumers of this country. Efficiency is needed by the farmer. But efficiency is needed also in all walks of life, and in no place more than in the Department of Finance, but I am afraid there are not many places where it is less shown.
We have heard references to after-the-war conditions, and, though I have little hope of seeing the war end as quickly as some people have, it is worth our while to consider the probable state of affairs after the war. There are troubles we shall have to bear, which will only begin after the war is over. In the first short session after the beginning of the war, we voted $50,000,000 for war expenses. A few months later we voted $100,000,000. In the session following we voted $250,000,000, and this session we have voted $500,000,000-ten times the amount of our first vote; and not a single vote of those I have mentioned has been less than double that which preceded it. I think the man would be rash who should say that we were not almost sure to have another vote in this House, with a strong probability that it will be double the last. I trust that will be the last we shall have, but of course we cannot be sure. All this means that we shall have

an extra indebtedness caused by the war of from $1,500,000,000 to $2,000,000,000. We shall also have a yearly pension list of $30,000,000 to $50,000,000. The man who thinks we are not liable to such an amount must be very sanguine as to the early end of the war. That means that we shall have to raise in the neighbourhood of $150,000,000 a year on account of the war alone, besides all that we must raise for other purposes. We hear the boast made that last year we had some $60,000,000 to the good, notwithstanding the fact that we paid $25,000,000 in interest on war indebtedness and pensions-$85,000,000 In all. But we must remember that in these years of war we are sure to be in a very much better position to pay large sums than we are likely to be afterwards. It has been admitted over and over again in this debate, that conditions are abnormal, that revenue and exports are abnormally large. I do not know what our exports of war material are, but I find that for the year 1916 our exports of cartridges alone amounted to about $225,000,000. It is plain that the only reason why our revenue exceeds our expenditure this year is to be found in these conditions, otherwise, we should be far behind, we should not have one cent of surplus to pay towards our indebtedness or pensions or interest on war debts.
The question of income tax has been discussed occasionally in this House. The Minister of Finance objects strongly to an income tax on account of the cost of collection, but I do not think he will deny that the cost of collecting an income tax is trifling compared with the direct and indirect cost of collecting customs taxes. The last year for which we have official figures of the manufactures of Canada is 1910. I find that during that year we manufactured goods to the value, approximately, of $1,166,000,000. Of these, we exported $144,000,000, leaving $1,022,000,000 of home manufactured goods to be consumed in Canada. Our imports of manufactured goodfs for the same year were nearly $255,000,000. I think we are safe in saying that, generally speaking, the same price is paid for home manufactured goods as for the imported goods. We paid an average duty on imported manufactured goods of about thirty per cent, as nearly as I can gather.
We have listened to the arguments of the Solicitor General on free wheat, and I think those arguments work in very well here. He told ^us that now that the duty is eliminated, the prices in the importing market are what they were before, less the

duty. That is the actual result he finds in the case of wheat. But the same would be the result in the case of imports of manufactured goods. If the Solicitor General is right in his contention, then, if we throw off the duty from $255,000,000 of imported manufactured goods, we decrease the price not only of those goods but of the home manufactured goods as well to the former level in the importing country less the duty. That is the Solicitor General's own argument in the case of wheat, and if it is a good argument it must apply to manufactured goods as well. We pay $30 of duty on every $100 worth of goods -we import. Then we pay about $3 more as a profit for the importer who pays the duty, making $33 on every $100 worth of goods. We consume of home manufactured1 goods about four times as much as we import, which would represent. higher prices equal to $132 for each $100 worth of imported goods. Adding this to the $33, you have $165 which we pay out in order that the revenue may receive $30. Is that efficiency? I submit it is not; it is the most wasteful way we could adopt for the collecting of revenues. Yet we follow this method at a time when it is most important that our methods should be efficient, and that for every dollar we pay in taxes as much as possible should go into the public treasury. People are beginning to recognize the iniquity of operation of the tariff, and the Toronto News, the chief journalistic spokesman in Canada, I suppose, of the manufacturers, as the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and. the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) are the chief spokesmen for protected interests in this House, has the following in its issue of 24th April, 1917:
Manufacturers and the Future.
If the Daily News may speak a word in season we would advise the Association to take every feasible means of justifying- fiscal protection as essential to Canadian industries, to the employees of these industries and to the country as a whole. For the most part the manufacturers have a good case and they should place it before the people in effective form. A tariff ferment is working. The Western farmers want lower duties, but on the other hand the war has brought a strong hope of inter-imperial and even inter-Ally trade arrangements supported by preferential tariffs. The Dominion could not prosper industrially without fiscal protection, and this is why the people support it. The system could never be maintained in the interests of the manufacturers alone, but as the manufacturers control the enterprises and business fostered by the tariff they should take the lead in making its advantages understood by the people.
62J
The manufactures pf Canada have never "been .slow in trying to educate the people upon the effects o-f protection. However, I think the News feels that they must be a little smarter about it, .that there is danger ahead, and that a tariff ferment is working. If the newspaper means that the people are thinking along tariff lines and are beginning to realize the iniquity of the tariff, it is quite right. I do not say that the customs tariff must at puce be completely abolished, but I say that a manufacturing industry which requires 30 per cent protection in this or any other country is not suited to the country and it is not in the interest of the country that it should be carried on. An industry that cannot thrive on a 10 pr 15 per cent tariff is not suited to the country and should not he continued. I believe that if we 'would make 15 per cent our maximum tariff rate we would have just as much manufacturing in Canada as we have now, Canada would be more prosperous and the wages paid would be better because we would only carry pn manufacturing industries that are suited to tile country. The people are thinking along tariff lines to-day. The sentiments expressed so forcibly here from time to time by my hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) are just the very sentiments that are filling the minds of the people from the Atlantic to the Pacific, not only the people on the western prairies, hut the people of the Maritime Provinces, Quebec and even a very large part of Ontario, protectionist as it is. It is a matter that is receiving a great deal of attention on the part of the people and they are realizing the iniquity pf the tariff.
I have been told by a prominent manufacturer in Canada that on some lines of manufacture where the duty is highest the manufacturers are making no money and that they must have more protection- to succeed. What does that mean? It means that while in some oases we pay $130 or $140 for goods that we cpuld buy but for the tariff for $100, we are paying that $30 or $40 -into the pockets of the Canadian manufacturers for the purpose of making millionaires while in other cases we are throwing the money away. If it is doing no -gpod at all we might as well throw it into the fire if my information is right. What is the use of paying these tremendous duties if they are doing no good? I would say at once, abolish these duties and let the manufacturers who are engaged in these lines of manufacture go at

some work that is suited to the country. The Solicitor General told us something in regard to the western free trade sentiments, and I 'believe he understands the subject. Some people suggest as a solution for this trouble the establishment of large manufacturing industries in the West. I think that probably the Solicitor General knows the difficulties in the way and that this is net a solution of the question. In conversation once with a prominent Conservative protectionist, he advanced the theory to me that the proper way to do was to establish a tariS between the . East and the West so that we could develop manufacturing industries in the West. If we established a tariff against the East we might have protection of the West against the East. If it is correct to say that manufacturing industries are essential to the East surely it is just as correct to say that they are essential to the West, with the tremendous capabilities of that country. We have a country which is capable of sustaining ten times the present population of Canada and we are told that in order to sustain a big population we must have manufacturing industries. I think my Conservative protectionist friend was not so very far astray if his views were right. But they are not correct. I. told him that he was following the protectionist argument to its legitimate conclusion, but that I had no use for his proposal.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: How does my hon. friend explain that Winnipeg is the third largest manufacturing city in Canada?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not propose to
enter into an argument with regard to Winnipeg, because Winnipeg is not a typical [DOT]city of the West. It has water powers which the rest of the country has not. The Solicitor General can answer that question better than I can. I am speaking for the large plain district west of Winnipeg. If my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) will come with me to southern Saskatchewan I can take him for days and weeks during the winter time and he cannot find a water power that will run a coffee mill. I think if he talked a little while to the Solicitor General he could put him right on that, and I think the Solicitor General would not for a moment advance that plan of solving the question. In Saskatchewan I have ripened tomatoes very successfully and I know that some people have ripened apples there. Our British Columbia friends tell us that in order to prevent the prairie farmers from eating American apples they must have a considerable amount of pro-

tection. We have as good a right to forbid our farmers eating British Columbia apples as the British Columbia men have to prevent us eating American apples. It would take far more protection to shut out British Columbia and American apple growers in favour of the Saskatchewan apple growers than it takes to shut out American apples from the prairies. But the theory is the same. If it is right in one case it is right in the other. Surely we have a right to our own market if we can grow enough " tomatoes to supply the demand in Saskatchewan. But, probably our consumers would.have to pay more for tomatoes and probably the men who grew tomatoes would do better if they were to go into some other line. Their case seems to me to be the same as that of the manufacturers who are not making any money. But then think of the home market right at our door, instead of going a thousand miles across plains, over mountains and through tunnels to get to that home market. If the argument is good in one case it is good in another. That is the sort of argument we continually hear in favour of protection, this blessed old home market out of which we can make so much money and out of which we never make anything. I do not believe in the theory that any one part of Canada should have protection against another. I do not believe in the theory that we should have this exorbitant protection in favour of any one class of people in Canada as against another. I believe we should produce things suitable to our own soil and climate and that we should buy other articles from those who are in a better position to produce them than we are. I believe different soils, different climates, different conditions and even different temperaments were given us for a great and wise purpose and I am sufficiently old fashioned in my belief to be satisfied that it is poor business kicking against the goads or against the Creator's plans.
In the year 1910, we manufactured goods for home consumption to the value of $1,022,000,000; and they say that we paid duty on the whole of this amount, eitheT into the treasury of the country or into the pockets of some one else, or else we threw it away in oases where the manufacturer was not making any money. We are told that this creates a wonderful home market for us. What about that home market? I find that to produce not only that $1,022,000,000 but the whole $1,166,000,000, wages and salaries are paid to the amount

of $241,000,000, less than 24 per cent of the cost of the manufactured goods. We are paying 25 per cent and 30 per cent on that in order to encourage the home manufacturer and to get the home market. That is, we pay $250,000,000 or $300,000,000 in order to get the home market of people who earn $240,000,000. Then where is the money going to come from? We will have to get more in actual profits than they actually earn in order to be even with the game. That is an exact fact. That was proved conclusively iby the Solicitor General in his free wheat argument, proved to the hilt. I believe that if we abolished our protection on a great many things and materially reduced it on other things we would still employ as many labourers as we do now, and would pay as good wages. President Wilson made a careful examination of the wages paid in highly protected manufac-utring industries and in those not so highly protected. He satisfied himself that in the lines where they had very little protection they paid higher wages than in those that were highly protected. I think there is no question about that. I once took occasion to look into that myself. I thought that I would get w*hat information I could as to the wages paid in Great Britain, in Prance and in Germany. As those three countries were naturally in pretty much the same position, the rate of wages, other circumstances being equal, would be about equal. I found that in free trade Great Britain the rate of wages was over 26 per cent higher than in either France or Germany. I found that in those two protectionist countries the rate of wages was practically the same, while in Great Britain it was 26 per cent higher. That bears out the contention of President Wilson that it is in the unprotected manufactures that the best wages are paid. That is quite natural because they are engaged in lines which are natural to the country. The others are not, and therefore are not able to pay such good wages.
The Solicitor General is rather troubled about the slowness of these British statesmen, who do not seem to be bright enough to know when to adopt protection or anything else. He is worried about the adverse balance of trade against them. On page 889 of Hansard, he enters into quite a wail with regard to the unfortunate position of those people in Great Britain. He laments that the balance of trade is against them, that they do not know enough to put on a protective duty, and adds:
That is the position she is in whereas, on the other hand, it is unfortunately true that her
rivals in this struggle have enormous balances of trade in their favour and have, within their own borders, every great industry brought to its highest point of perfection. That is one of the great elemental truths that has enabled Germany to maintain the struggle to this day.
Either the Solicitor General is astray in his statement, or the bluebooks which his Government publishes are seriously astray.
I find, in the last Trade and Commerce reports which are available, that Germany during the five years immediately preceding the war, imported during every year much more than she exported. I find that for those five years her imports exceeded her exports by 7,400,000,000 marks, about $1,800,000,000, or $360,000,000, a year on an average. That is protectionist Germany which my hon. friend wants to hold up as an example of a country having a trade balance in its favour.

It is unfortunately true that her rivals in this struggle have enormous balances of trade in their favour, and have, within their own borders-
And so on. Now what balance of trade Germany has in her favour since the war began I do not think my hon. friend knows; I do not, because we cannot know exactly what is going on in that country, as Germany is not giving out any such information. I have quoted up to the time of the war, and in all these years the balance of trade was against Germany.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It is true that in the last years she had not been gaining very rapidly. For one year before the war she had made a big jump. I have looked up the figures for the last ten or fifteen years, and I have found that the average is about the same as it was during those five years, a little less, I think, so that she has not been gaining. She may have gained in one year, but you cannot prove'things by one quotation. One swallow does not make a summer, although, if my hon. friend so desired, he could prove to his own satisfaction that one swallow made half a dozen summers.
I was dealing with the question of free wheat and of my hon. friend's proof of the statement that we were getting no benefit on the higher grades of wheat. He claims

to prove that by the conditions of the market for one day. I have read a great many opinions of experts in the grain trade, hundreds of which opinions are quoted in the newspapers, and I do not remember seeing a single one that claimed for a moment that the market quotations of the day cited by my hon. friend prove anything, although he says that they prove everything; that they settle the whole question. I submit it does not; the mere fact that there were certain spreads on one day proves nothing. I might just as well claim that because the prices are to-day from 40 to 50 cents a bushel higher than they were at the time the Order in Council was passed, therefore the prices have advanced on account of wheat being put on the free list. The experts do not contend for a moment that the quotations of that day prove anything. Mr. James Car-ruthers, in the Financial Post of the 28th of April, speaking of free wheat, says:
I believe it will prove a great benefit to our farmers. Free wheat will contribute to the prosperity of the western farmer, and consequently to his contentment.
I fancy, if I am not mistaken, that Mr. Carruthers was an expert in grain matters when my hon. friend was running around in pantaloons, although ,my hon. friend thinks that he knows more than Mr. *Carruthers about this .subject. I quote from the Nor-West Farmer of the 20th of April:
Regarding- the permanent benefits of the removal of the duty on wheat, only time can actually determine.
My hon. friend, however, thinks he can determine it from one day's quotations.
_ It will mean much to the western farmers; it will give them this great southern market at their very door, which will be utilized whenever it is advantageous to do so. This will be a permanent advantage.
My hon. friend says it is at present advantageous for him to have free wheat on account of the low grades of wheat, and I grant he is right; but it is advantageous for him to have it at all times, because of the fact that our highest grade of wheat, which is better than anything the American farmer produces, is wanted at all times by the Minneapolis miller for mixing purposes, and he is always willing to pay a little extra price for it, so if we always have that market we shall always get that benefit. I do not purpose saying anything further about this Order in Council or Statute. I tried to secure a little information from my hon. friend when

he was speaking, when he claimed that the Order in Council wa3 in exactly the same position as a statute. I asked him if the Order in Council could not be repealed at any momnt by another Order in Council, and he admitted that it could. I am not sure whether he meant by the further answer that he made, to leave the impression that if a statute were passed, it could also be repealed by an Order in Council. My hon. friend may be a little rash sometimes and so may his Government, but they would hardly -be so rash as to repeal, by an Order in Council, an Act passed by this House shortly before. I am not, however, going to enter into a discussion as to whether or not an Act of Parliament passed in this way could be repealed by an Order in Council.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It certainly could not
be repealed unless the statute itself provided for that being done.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am not going to
enter into a discussion of the effect of this Order in Council when the war is ended. Personally, I believe my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is right so far as I have been able to follow his argument. I am very glad that the Government have gone so far as they have in the matter of free wheat, although I am very sorry for the way in which we were given free wheat, and I am very sorry that they should have waited until a moment when the placing of wheat on the free list would do the least good, although I am not saying this in a complaining way. Some statements have been made in this House as to the proportion of wheat still in the farmers' hands at the time the Order in Council was passed. The proportion of wheat was very small; but the proportion of low grade wheat is very much smaller, for this reason. The parts of the country in which there were the poorer grades had very light crops, and consequently the farmers did not take long to thresh the grain, and as they needed the money, they marketed those low grades quickly. I believe, therefore, the greater proportion of that grain was marketed and that a very small proportion of it is left in the farmers' hands. The great benefit from free wheat has gone, for this year at least, to the speculator and the miller, and hardly any of it to the farmer. Although I know a few farmers in my constituency who are still holding wheat, I do not know of one who is holding the low grade of wheat.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think the Government crop reports would lead one to suppose

there is quite a large amount of wheat still in the farmers' hands. I am not saying this as a matter of criticism, but just as a matter of information. Does my hon. friend think that statement is not correct?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
From what I know,
there is a very small proportion of wheat in the farmers' hands now. Although the bulk may be considerable, it is a very small proportion of the crop. It must be remembered that the official reports to which my hon. friend refers were made some time ago, and that the wheat is continually and rapidly going out of the farmers' hands, because in the latter part of the winter most of the grain is rushed off. The farmers must market it before the sleighing is over, because after that they have no opportunity until after the seeding is done, and then they are busy ploughing. It is a rash thing for a farmer to hold grain over unless he has an elevator. Some of them are holding grain in elevators, but that is a very small proportion of the crop, and so far as the low grades of wheat are concerned, there is practically none now in the farmers^ hands, so that whatever benefit is derived must be derived entirely by the speculators and practically none by the farmers. I think the Solicitor General will bear me out in that.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Not yet.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I tried to draw out the Minister of Finance this evening, but evidently he does not want to be drawn. We have heard, however, what the Solicitor General has to say; it was pretty carefully worded, and it might mean almost anything or nothing. We have also heard what the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Morris) has to say. He was very outspoken; I aim afraid he blurted the truth right out. He accused us of being untruthful. I could not accuse him of that, because I think he told ue the plain truth. This is purely an emergency measure, and the moment it suits the Government they will rescind it.
If the free wheat policy is to be of benefit only in the case of lower grades of wheat, what will happen if we have a good crop this year? Last year our crop was very poor on account of the rust, but this year we may have a good one, plump grain, I hope, like we had in 1915. What would happen in that case? If the Government are thoroughly sincere, and I would not like to accuse them of being insincere, why then at the beginning of next season they will
rescind the order; they must, if their reasoning is sound.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: You have the positive statement of the Minister of Finance that he will not do that.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I was not in the House when the Minister of Finance made that positive statement, and I have tried to draw him out this evening but he will not be drawn. There have been eo many interpretations of that positive statement of his, that I do not know what it means. I am told that it was merely a statement that the Order in Council would not be rescinded except on authority from this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read Hansard to-morrow, he will see that he has not correctly quoted me.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
In the meantime, we
have the positive statement of hon. gentlemen opposite that it is an emergency measure, and we have the rather roundabout statement of the Solicitor General from which the only reasonable inference is that the Order in Council will be repealed when it is no longer required, and it will be no longer required if we have no low grade wheat this year. I hope we will have none, but I do not want to see this Order repealed.
On motion of Mr. Bou.lay, the debate was adjourned.
On the motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 11.20 p.m.
Wednesday, May 2, 1917.
